Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 76, verses 1–12 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: it is Madani.
Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it is Makki.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. It was also said that the part of it from His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages﴾, to the end of the surah, is Makki, and what precedes it is Madani.
Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "A man from Abyssinia came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Ask and inquire.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have been given preference over us in colours, forms and prophethood. Tell me, if I believe in what you believe in and act by what you act by, shall I be with you in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand my soul is, indeed the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years.' Then he said: 'Whoever says, "There is no god but Allah," has a covenant with Allah; and whoever says, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," there will be written for him one hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand good deeds.' And this surah was revealed: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾ up to His saying ﴿and a great kingdom﴾. The Abyssinian said: 'And will my eye see what your eyes see in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he suffered until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: 'Indeed I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand.'"
Ahmad in al-Zuhd narrated from Muhammad ibn Mutarrif, who said: "The trustworthy one narrated to me that a black man used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about tasbih and tahlil. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to him: 'You have asked the Messenger of Allah too much.' He said: 'Mah, O ʿUmar!' And upon the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾, until when it reached the mention of Paradise, the black man sighed a sigh and his soul departed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'He died out of longing for Paradise.'"
Ibn Wahb narrated something similar from Ibn Zayd, as a mursal marfu" report.
Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Munayʿ, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ until he finished it, then said: 'Indeed I see what you do not see and hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has a right to creak; there is not a space of four fingers in it but an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah. By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not enjoy women on beds, and you would go out to the high roads, crying out to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.'"

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes and the scholars of meanings that "hal" here means "qad" and is not an interrogative. Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu ʿUbaydah said this.
Al-Farra' said: "Hal" can be a negation and can be a statement; this is from the statement form, because you say: "Hal a'taytuka?" (Have I not given you?), affirming that you gave him. Negation is when you say: "Hal yaqdiru ahadun ʿala mithl hadha?" (Can anyone do the like of this?). It was also said that although it means "qad," it contains the sense of interrogation. The original is "a-hal atā," so the meaning is "a-qad atā," and the interrogation is for confirmation and approximation. The intended "insan" here is Adam, according to Qatadah, al-Thawri, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi and others. ﴿A period of time﴾: it was said it is forty years before the spirit was breathed into him. It was also said that he was created from clay for forty years, then from black mud shaped (ḥama' masnun) for forty years, then from dry clay (ṣalṣal) for forty years, so his creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years.
It was also said that the "ḥin" mentioned here has no known measure. It was said the intended "insan" is the children of Adam, and "ḥin" is the period of gestation. The clause ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from "insan," or in a position of nominative as an attribute of "ḥin."
Al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab said: the meaning is that he was a formed body of dirt and clay, not mentioned, not known, and not known what his name was or what was meant by him; then the spirit was breathed into him and he became something mentioned.
Yahya ibn Salam said: ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ in creation, though he was a thing worth mentioning with Allah. It was also said that the intended "dhikr" here is not informing, for Allah's informing about creatures is eternal; rather it is "dhikr" in the sense of standing and nobility, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾.
Al-Qushayri said: he was not mentioned to creation, though he was mentioned to Allah, glory be to Him.
Al-Farra' said: he was a thing but was not mentioned.
Thus the negation was directed to the restriction.
It was also said the meaning is: periods of time have passed, and Adam was not a thing, nor created, nor mentioned to anyone of the creation.
Muqatil said: there is preceding and following in the speech, and its estimation is: "Has there come upon man a period of time in which he was not a thing worth mentioning?" because He created him after creating all living beings and did not create any living being after him.
﴿Indeed We created man from a drop of fluid﴾: the intended "insan" here is the son of Adam.
Al-Qurtubi said: without disagreement. The nutfah is the water that drips, which is semen, and every small amount of water in a vessel is a nutfah; its plural is nutaf. "Amshaj" is an attribute of "nutfah," and it is the plural of mashij or mashij, meaning mixtures. The intended meaning is the male's nutfah and the female's nutfah and their mixing.
It is said: "masha/a hadha bi-hadha fa-huwa mamshuj," meaning this was mixed with that, so it is mixed.
Al-Mubarrad said: "masha yamshu," when it mixes; here it is the mixing of the nutfah with blood.
Ru'bah ibn al-ʿAjjaj said:
"They cast every premature, mixed one, which has not been clothed with skin of mixed blood."
Al-Farra' said: "amshaj" is the mixing of the man's water, the woman's water, the blood and the clot. It is said "masha hadha" when he mixed. It was also said that "amshaj" is redness in whiteness and whiteness in redness. Al-Qurtubi said: this is an opinion that many lexicographers prefer.
Al-Hudhali said:
"As if the feathers and the sinew of it were the binding of the blade, tied to it with a mashij."
That is because the man's water is white and thick, and the woman's water is yellow and thin, and the child is created from both.
Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-amshaj" are the mixtures, because they are blended from kinds from which man is created and from differing natures.
It was also said that "amshaj" is a singular word like "birmat a'shar," and this is supported by its occurrence as an adjective of "nutfah." The clause ﴿We test him﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "khalaqna," that is, intending to test him; and it may be a circumstantial clause from "insan," meaning: We test him with good and evil and with obligations.
Al-Farra' said: its meaning, and Allah knows best, is ﴿so We made him hearing and seeing﴾; "nabtalihi" is a preceding clause whose meaning is delayed, because testing does not occur except after the completion of creation, and on this view this circumstance is presumed (muqaddarah); it was also said it is concurrent (muqarinah).
It was also said the meaning of testing is transferring him from one state to another, in the manner of metaphor, but the first is preferable.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that He gave him what makes testing valid, saying: ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful﴾; that is, We made clear to him and made him know the path of guidance and misguidance, and good and evil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. Mujahid said: that is, We made clear the way to misery and happiness.
Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: the "sabil" here is his coming out of the womb. It was also said it is its benefits and harms by which he is guided by his nature and perfect intellect. The accusatives "shakiran" and "kafuran" are circumstantial from the object of "hadaynahu": that is, We enabled him to travel the path in both of his states together. It was also said they are circumstantial from "sabil" metaphorically: that is, We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way.
Makki related from the Kufans that "imma" here is conditional "in" with "ma" added after it: that is, We made the way clear to him, if he is grateful and if he is ungrateful.
Al-Farra' chose this, but the Basrans do not permit it, because the conditional "in" does not enter upon nouns except when a verb is implied after it, and it is not valid here to imply a verb, because then "shakiran" and "kafuran" would have to be nominative.
It is possible to imply a verb that governs "shakiran" and "kafuran," its estimation being: if We created him grateful, then he is grateful; and if We created him disbelieving, then he is disbelieving. This is according to the reading of the majority, ﴿imma shakiran wa-imma kafuran﴾, with the hamza of "imma" kasra.
Abu al-Simak and Abu al-ʿAjjaj read it with fatha. On the fatha reading, "imma" is the coordinating particle in the dialect of some Arabs, or it is the detailing "imma," whose answer is implied. It was also said "shakiran" and "kafuran" are accusative by implying "kana," the estimation being: whether he was grateful or he was ungrateful.
Then He, glory be to Him, explained what He prepared for the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Indeed We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blaze﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Hisham from Ibn ʿAmir read "salasila" with tanwin; Qunbul, on stopping, from Ibn Kathir, and Hamzah stopped without alif; and the rest stopped with alif.
The reasoning of those who read "salasila" with tanwin, despite its having the form of the diptote plurals, is that they intended harmony, because what precedes it, ﴿imma shakiran wa-imma kafuran﴾, and what follows it, "aghlalan wa-sa'iran," are tanwined; or it is according to the dialect of those who make all diptotes triptote, as al-Kisa'i and others of the Kufans related from some Arabs.
Al-Akhfash said: we have heard from the Arabs one who makes triptote every diptote, because the original in nouns is triptote, and the non-triptote is left out due to an accidental factor in them.
Al-Farra' said: it is according to the dialect of those who put all nouns in the genitive, except the saying "hu azrafu minka" (he is more refined than you), for they do not put it in the genitive. Ibn al-Anbari cited in this regard the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:
"As if our swords among us and among them were batons in the hands of players."
From it is the saying of a poet:
"And when the men see Yazid, you see them, humbled of necks, lowering of gazes."
With a kasra on the sin of "nawakis." And the saying of Labid:
"And the hard-worn curtains, they call upon her for her doom, with fastenings whose hooks are similar."
And also his saying:
"Bounty, and one of generosity who helps toward liberality, gracious, mixing with the desires of its flocks."
It was also said that the tanwin is for agreement with the orthography of the Makki, Madani and Kufan codices, for they have it with an alif. It was also said that this tanwin is a substitute for the vowel of pausal lengthening (harf al-itlaq), and the connected reading runs like the pause. "Salasil" has already been explained, and the difference concerning it is whether they are the fetters, or what is placed on the necks, as in the saying of the poet:
". . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
But the chains and the shackles have encircled the necks."
"Aghlal" is the plural of "ghull," by which hands are bound to the necks. "Sa'ir" is intense fuel, and the explanation of "sa'ir" has already preceded.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He prepared for the grateful, saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous will drink from a cup﴾. "Al-abrar" are the people of obedience and sincerity; "al-sadq" is the plural of barr or barir.
Al-Sihah says: the plural of "al-barr" is "al-abrar," and the plural of "al-barr" (the dutiful one) is "al-barara," and it is said: "fulan yabarru khaliqahu wa-yabrurahu," that is, he obeys Him.
Al-Hasan said: "al-barr" is one who does not harm even an ant.
Qatadah said: "al-abrar" are those who fulfill Allah's right and keep their vows.
(p-1564) The "ka's" in the language is the vessel in which there is drink; if there is no drink in it, it is not called a "ka's." There is no basis for restricting it to glass; rather it may be of glass, of gold, of silver, of porcelain and other things, and the cups of the Arabs were of different kinds. The word "ka's" may also be applied to the wine itself, as in the saying of the poet:
"And a cup I drank with pleasure, and another by which I treated myself."
﴿Its mixture will be camphor﴾: that is, it is mixed with it and blended with it. It is said "mazajahu yamzujuhu mazjan," that is, he mixed it, he mixes it, mixing. From it is the saying of the poet:
"As if a jar from the house of Ra's, as if its blend were honey and water."
And the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:
"You turned the cup away from us, Umm ʿAmr, while the cup used to run to us on the right."
"Aged, as if the herbs in it, when water mixes with it, were heated."
From it comes the "mizaj" of the body, which is what is mixed into it of humours. As for "al-kafur," it was said: it is the name of a spring in Paradise called "al-Kafuri," by whose water the wine of Paradise is blended.
Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is blended for them with camphor, and sealed for them with musk.
ʿIkrimah said: its "mizaj" is its taste. It was also said that the camphor is only in its scent, not in its taste.

It was also said that he meant camphor in its whiteness, the fineness of its fragrance, and its coolness, because camphor is not drunk, as in His saying: ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "as fire."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Musk, camphor and ginger perfumed it."

Muqatil said: "It is not the camphor of this world. God named what is with Him by what is with you so that hearts may be guided to it." The clause is in the position of a genitive qualifier (sifah) for "a cup."

It was also said that "kana" (was) here is redundant, meaning: "from a cup whose mixture is camphor."

﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾: ʿaynan (a spring) is in the accusative because it is a badal (substitute) for kafuran (camphor), since its water is as white as camphor.

Makki said: it is a badal from the position of "min kas" (from a cup), with an omitted mudaf (qualified noun), as if it were said: "They drink a wine whose wine is of a spring." It was also said that it is accusative as the object of "yashrabun" (they drink), meaning "a spring from a cup." It was also said that it is accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), as al-Akhfash said. It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb explained by what follows, meaning: "They drink a spring from which the servants of God drink." The first view is the better one, and the clause ﴿from which the servants of God drink﴾ is a qualifier of ʿaynan.

It was also said that the preposition (ba') in ﴿drink from it﴾ is redundant. It was also said that it means "min" (from), as al-Zajjaj said, and the reading of Ibn Abi ʿAbla supports this: "yashrabuha ʿibadu Allah" (the servants of God drink it).

It was also said that "yashrabu" (drink) is taken to include the sense of "yaltadhdhu" (delight in), and it was also said that the phrase is connected to "yashrabu," with the pronoun referring back to the cup.

Al-Farra' said: "yashrabuha" and "yashrabu biha" are the same in meaning, and it seems that "yashrabu biha" means "they are quenched by it and benefit from it." He recited the verse of al-Hudhali:

"They drank with sea water, then they rose up."

He said: "Similar to it is: 'He spoke with a good speech' and 'He spoke a good speech.'"

﴿They make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾: meaning they lead it wherever they wish and benefit from it as they please, and its water follows them to every place they want it to reach. They split it, as a river is split and made to gush here and there.

Mujahid said: "They lead it wherever they wish, and it follows them wherever they turn; it turns with them." This clause is another qualifier of ʿaynan.

﴿They fulfil their vows﴾: this clause is a new sentence (isti'naf) that explains the reason for which they were given what was mentioned, and so is what is conjoined to it. The meaning of "nadhr" (vow) linguistically is obligation, and the meaning is: they fulfil what God has made obligatory upon them of acts of obedience.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: they fulfil the obedience of God, such as prayer, pilgrimage and the like.

Ikrimah said: they fulfil when they vow in the right of God, glorified is He. In the Shari'ah, a vow is what a responsible person makes obligatory upon himself, so the meaning is: they fulfil what they have made obligatory upon themselves.

Al-Farra' said: there is an implied element in the speech, meaning: they used to fulfil vows in the world.

Al-Kalbi said: "They fulfil the covenant," meaning they complete the covenant.

The better reading of "vow" here is what the servant makes obligatory upon himself, without restriction.

﴿And they fear a day whose evil will be widespread﴾: the intended day is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of its evil being "istitarah" (spreading) is its being widespread and dispersed. It is said: "istatara yastiru istitarah, fahuwa mustatir," and it is the form "istaf'ala" from "tayaran" (flying). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She spent the night, having stirred in the heart a crack, despite her distance, spreading."

The Arabs say: "The crack spread in the flask or the bottle" when it extends, and it is said: "al-harig istatar" (the fire spread) when it spreads.

Al-Farra' said: "al-mustatir" means "al-mustatil" (extended).

Qatadah said: the evil of that day spread until it filled the heavens and the earth.

Muqatil said: its evil was pervasive in the heavens, so they were split, the stars were scattered, and the angels were terrified; and on earth the mountains were blown away and the waters sank.

﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive﴾: meaning they feed these three categories the food, despite their love for it and its scarcity among them.

Mujahid said: "Despite its scarcity, their love for it and their desire for it." So His saying "ʿala hubbihi" (in spite of their love for it) is in the accusative position as a hal (circumstantial clause), meaning: they, while loving it. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92]. It was also said: "in spite of love of giving food, out of their eagerness for good." Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: "In spite of love of giving food."

It was also said that the pronoun in "hubbihi" refers to God: meaning they give food, giving it out of love for God; that is, they give food out of love of God.

This is supported by His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾.

The miskin (needy) is one in misery (maskanah), who is poor, or one who is poorer than the poor. By the orphan is meant the orphans of the Muslims. The captive is one who is taken captive and then confined.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: the captive is the one confined.

Ikrimah said: the captive is the slave.

Abu Hamzah al-Thumali said: the captive is the woman.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the verse of charity (sadaqat) and the verse of the sword abrogated (naskh) this feeding concerning the captive who is a disbeliever. Others said: rather, it is muhkam (not abrogated), and feeding the needy and the orphan is voluntary, while feeding the captive is to preserve his life until the ruler decides concerning him.

The clause ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾ is in the accusative position as a hal, with an implied verb of saying: meaning they say, "We only feed you," or they are saying, "We only feed you." This means that they do not expect repayment and do not want the people's praise for it, nor do they seek to be completed by it through this; but God knew it from their hearts and praised them for it.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: they did not say this, but God knew it from their hearts and praised them, and from His praise it is known that they did this [p. 1565] out of fear of God and hope for His reward.

﴿We do not want from you any reward or thanks﴾: meaning we do not seek from you repayment for this feeding, nor do we want thanks from you to us; rather it is purely for the sake of God. This sentence confirms what precedes it, because whoever feeds for the sake of God does not want repayment and does not seek thanks from the one he feeds.

﴿Indeed we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾: meaning we fear the punishment of a day characterised by these two qualities. The meaning of "ʿabusan" (austere) is that it is a day on which faces frown from its terror and severity, so the meaning is: it has frowning.

Al-Farra', Abu ʿUbayda and al-Mubarrad said: "yawman qamtariran" and "qumatir" are used when it is difficult and severe. Al-Farra' recited:

"Sons of our paternal uncle, do you remember our trial against you on the day of Qumatir?"

Al-Akhfash said: "al-qamtarir" is the most intense and longest of days in trial. From this is the saying of the poet:

"So flee when the war has raised its dust, and the austere, qumatir day has persisted in it."

Al-Kisa'i said: "iqmatarra al-yawm wa izmaharra" means when the day is difficult and severe. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Sons of war, we bequeathed to them a qamtarah, and whoever meets from us on that day will flee."

Mujahid said: "The frowning is with the two lips, and the qitmir is with the forehead and the eyebrows," so he made them attributes of one changed on that day because of what he sees of the hardships. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"He is able to hunt with a broken stick, and he is contracted for an hour and frowning."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "Qamtarir" means contracted between the two eyes and the eyebrows.

Al-Zajjaj said: "iqmatarrat al-naqah" is said when the she-camel raises her tail, gathers her two teats, and throws out with her nose what the drops of milk precede; and he took the mim to be an added letter.

﴿So God protected them from the evil of that day﴾: meaning He gave them, instead of the frowning which the disbelievers have, brightness in the faces and joy in the hearts.

Al-Dahhak said: "Nadrah" is whiteness and purity in their faces.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is beauty and radiance. It was also said: nadrah is the trace of blessing.

﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured﴾: meaning because of their patience in the obligations. It was also said: patience in poverty; it was also said: patience in hunger; it was also said: patience in fasting.

The better reading of the verse is that it refers to patience in everything in which patience is an act of obedience to God, glorified is He. "Ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and the implied meaning is: "for their patience." ﴿A garden and silk﴾: meaning He caused them to enter the Garden and clothed them in silk, which is the clothing of the people of the Garden, in place of leaving it in this world in compliance with what came in the Shari'ah concerning its prohibition.

The apparent generality of these verses covers everyone who fears the Day of Resurrection, feeds for the sake of God, and fears His punishment. Although the cause (sabab) is specific, as will come, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, and the cause of revelation enters under its generality as a primary entry.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man﴾: he said: "Every man."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: "amshaj" (mingled), he said: "Its amshaj are its veins."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim related: "amshaj," he said: "the veins."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿from a drop of mingled fluid﴾, he said: "The fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman when they mix."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "amshaj" means colours: the man's drop is white and red, and the woman's drop is green and red.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, he said: "al-amshaj is what comes out after urine like pieces of strings, and from it the child is formed."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, concerning His saying: "and a captive," he said: "He is the polytheist."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning His saying: 'a needy one' he said: 'poor'; 'an orphan' he said: 'one without a father'; 'a captive' he said: 'the slave and the prisoner.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿And they give food﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: "This verse was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿a day austere﴾, he said: "Narrow." "Qamtarir," he said: "long."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas ibn Malik, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying: ﴿a day austere and distressing﴾, he said: 'It contracts what is between the eyes.'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Qamtarir is the man contracted between his two eyes and his face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: ﴿And He gave them brightness and joy﴾, he said: "Brightness in their faces and joy in their breasts."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 76, verses 1–12 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: it is Madani.
Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it is Makki.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. It was also said that the part of it from His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages﴾, to the end of the surah, is Makki, and what precedes it is Madani.
Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "A man from Abyssinia came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Ask and inquire.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have been given preference over us in colours, forms and prophethood. Tell me, if I believe in what you believe in and act by what you act by, shall I be with you in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand my soul is, indeed the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years.' Then he said: 'Whoever says, "There is no god but Allah," has a covenant with Allah; and whoever says, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," there will be written for him one hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand good deeds.' And this surah was revealed: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾ up to His saying ﴿and a great kingdom﴾. The Abyssinian said: 'And will my eye see what your eyes see in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he suffered until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: 'Indeed I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand.'"
Ahmad in al-Zuhd narrated from Muhammad ibn Mutarrif, who said: "The trustworthy one narrated to me that a black man used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about tasbih and tahlil. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to him: 'You have asked the Messenger of Allah too much.' He said: 'Mah, O ʿUmar!' And upon the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾, until when it reached the mention of Paradise, the black man sighed a sigh and his soul departed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'He died out of longing for Paradise.'"
Ibn Wahb narrated something similar from Ibn Zayd, as a mursal marfu" report.
Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Munayʿ, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ until he finished it, then said: 'Indeed I see what you do not see and hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has a right to creak; there is not a space of four fingers in it but an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah. By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not enjoy women on beds, and you would go out to the high roads, crying out to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.'"

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes and the scholars of meanings that "hal" here means "qad" and is not an interrogative. Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu ʿUbaydah said this.
Al-Farra' said: "Hal" can be a negation and can be a statement; this is from the statement form, because you say: "Hal a'taytuka?" (Have I not given you?), affirming that you gave him. Negation is when you say: "Hal yaqdiru ahadun ʿala mithl hadha?" (Can anyone do the like of this?). It was also said that although it means "qad," it contains the sense of interrogation. The original is "a-hal atā," so the meaning is "a-qad atā," and the interrogation is for confirmation and approximation. The intended "insan" here is Adam, according to Qatadah, al-Thawri, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi and others. ﴿A period of time﴾: it was said it is forty years before the spirit was breathed into him. It was also said that he was created from clay for forty years, then from black mud shaped (ḥama' masnun) for forty years, then from dry clay (ṣalṣal) for forty years, so his creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years.
It was also said that the "ḥin" mentioned here has no known measure. It was said the intended "insan" is the children of Adam, and "ḥin" is the period of gestation. The clause ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from "insan," or in a position of nominative as an attribute of "ḥin."
Al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab said: the meaning is that he was a formed body of dirt and clay, not mentioned, not known, and not known what his name was or what was meant by him; then the spirit was breathed into him and he became something mentioned.
Yahya ibn Salam said: ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ in creation, though he was a thing worth mentioning with Allah. It was also said that the intended "dhikr" here is not informing, for Allah's informing about creatures is eternal; rather it is "dhikr" in the sense of standing and nobility, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾.
Al-Qushayri said: he was not mentioned to creation, though he was mentioned to Allah, glory be to Him.
Al-Farra' said: he was a thing but was not mentioned.
Thus the negation was directed to the restriction.
It was also said the meaning is: periods of time have passed, and Adam was not a thing, nor created, nor mentioned to anyone of the creation.
Muqatil said: there is preceding and following in the speech, and its estimation is: "Has there come upon man a period of time in which he was not a thing worth mentioning?" because He created him after creating all living beings and did not create any living being after him.
﴿Indeed We created man from a drop of fluid﴾: the intended "insan" here is the son of Adam.
Al-Qurtubi said: without disagreement. The nutfah is the water that drips, which is semen, and every small amount of water in a vessel is a nutfah; its plural is nutaf. "Amshaj" is an attribute of "nutfah," and it is the plural of mashij or mashij, meaning mixtures. The intended meaning is the male's nutfah and the female's nutfah and their mixing.
It is said: "masha/a hadha bi-hadha fa-huwa mamshuj," meaning this was mixed with that, so it is mixed.
Al-Mubarrad said: "masha yamshu," when it mixes; here it is the mixing of the nutfah with blood.
Ru'bah ibn al-ʿAjjaj said:
"They cast every premature, mixed one, which has not been clothed with skin of mixed blood."
Al-Farra' said: "amshaj" is the mixing of the man's water, the woman's water, the blood and the clot. It is said "masha hadha" when he mixed. It was also said that "amshaj" is redness in whiteness and whiteness in redness. Al-Qurtubi said: this is an opinion that many lexicographers prefer.
Al-Hudhali said:
"As if the feathers and the sinew of it were the binding of the blade, tied to it with a mashij."
That is because the man's water is white and thick, and the woman's water is yellow and thin, and the child is created from both.
Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-amshaj" are the mixtures, because they are blended from kinds from which man is created and from differing natures.
It was also said that "amshaj" is a singular word like "birmat a'shar," and this is supported by its occurrence as an adjective of "nutfah." The clause ﴿We test him﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "khalaqna," that is, intending to test him; and it may be a circumstantial clause from "insan," meaning: We test him with good and evil and with obligations.
Al-Farra' said: its meaning, and Allah knows best, is ﴿so We made him hearing and seeing﴾; "nabtalihi" is a preceding clause whose meaning is delayed, because testing does not occur except after the completion of creation, and on this view this circumstance is presumed (muqaddarah); it was also said it is concurrent (muqarinah).
It was also said the meaning of testing is transferring him from one state to another, in the manner of metaphor, but the first is preferable.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that He gave him what makes testing valid, saying: ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful﴾; that is, We made clear to him and made him know the path of guidance and misguidance, and good and evil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. Mujahid said: that is, We made clear the way to misery and happiness.
Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: the "sabil" here is his coming out of the womb. It was also said it is its benefits and harms by which he is guided by his nature and perfect intellect. The accusatives "shakiran" and "kafuran" are circumstantial from the object of "hadaynahu": that is, We enabled him to travel the path in both of his states together. It was also said they are circumstantial from "sabil" metaphorically: that is, We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way.
Makki related from the Kufans that "imma" here is conditional "in" with "ma" added after it: that is, We made the way clear to him, if he is grateful and if he is ungrateful.
Al-Farra' chose this, but the Basrans do not permit it, because the conditional "in" does not enter upon nouns except when a verb is implied after it, and it is not valid here to imply a verb, because then "shakiran" and "kafuran" would have to be nominative.
It is possible to imply a verb that governs "shakiran" and "kafuran," its estimation being: if We created him grateful, then he is grateful; and if We created him disbelieving, then he is disbelieving. This is according to the reading of the majority, ﴿imma shakiran wa-imma kafuran﴾, with the hamza of "imma" kasra.
Abu al-Simak and Abu al-ʿAjjaj read it with fatha. On the fatha reading, "imma" is the coordinating particle in the dialect of some Arabs, or it is the detailing "imma," whose answer is implied. It was also said "shakiran" and "kafuran" are accusative by implying "kana," the estimation being: whether he was grateful or he was ungrateful.
Then He, glory be to Him, explained what He prepared for the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Indeed We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blaze﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Hisham from Ibn ʿAmir read "salasila" with tanwin; Qunbul, on stopping, from Ibn Kathir, and Hamzah stopped without alif; and the rest stopped with alif.
The reasoning of those who read "salasila" with tanwin, despite its having the form of the diptote plurals, is that they intended harmony, because what precedes it, ﴿imma shakiran wa-imma kafuran﴾, and what follows it, "aghlalan wa-sa'iran," are tanwined; or it is according to the dialect of those who make all diptotes triptote, as al-Kisa'i and others of the Kufans related from some Arabs.
Al-Akhfash said: we have heard from the Arabs one who makes triptote every diptote, because the original in nouns is triptote, and the non-triptote is left out due to an accidental factor in them.
Al-Farra' said: it is according to the dialect of those who put all nouns in the genitive, except the saying "hu azrafu minka" (he is more refined than you), for they do not put it in the genitive. Ibn al-Anbari cited in this regard the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:
"As if our swords among us and among them were batons in the hands of players."
From it is the saying of a poet:
"And when the men see Yazid, you see them, humbled of necks, lowering of gazes."
With a kasra on the sin of "nawakis." And the saying of Labid:
"And the hard-worn curtains, they call upon her for her doom, with fastenings whose hooks are similar."
And also his saying:
"Bounty, and one of generosity who helps toward liberality, gracious, mixing with the desires of its flocks."
It was also said that the tanwin is for agreement with the orthography of the Makki, Madani and Kufan codices, for they have it with an alif. It was also said that this tanwin is a substitute for the vowel of pausal lengthening (harf al-itlaq), and the connected reading runs like the pause. "Salasil" has already been explained, and the difference concerning it is whether they are the fetters, or what is placed on the necks, as in the saying of the poet:
". . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
But the chains and the shackles have encircled the necks."
"Aghlal" is the plural of "ghull," by which hands are bound to the necks. "Sa'ir" is intense fuel, and the explanation of "sa'ir" has already preceded.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He prepared for the grateful, saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous will drink from a cup﴾. "Al-abrar" are the people of obedience and sincerity; "al-sadq" is the plural of barr or barir.
Al-Sihah says: the plural of "al-barr" is "al-abrar," and the plural of "al-barr" (the dutiful one) is "al-barara," and it is said: "fulan yabarru khaliqahu wa-yabrurahu," that is, he obeys Him.
Al-Hasan said: "al-barr" is one who does not harm even an ant.
Qatadah said: "al-abrar" are those who fulfill Allah's right and keep their vows.
(p-1564) The "ka's" in the language is the vessel in which there is drink; if there is no drink in it, it is not called a "ka's." There is no basis for restricting it to glass; rather it may be of glass, of gold, of silver, of porcelain and other things, and the cups of the Arabs were of different kinds. The word "ka's" may also be applied to the wine itself, as in the saying of the poet:
"And a cup I drank with pleasure, and another by which I treated myself."
﴿Its mixture will be camphor﴾: that is, it is mixed with it and blended with it. It is said "mazajahu yamzujuhu mazjan," that is, he mixed it, he mixes it, mixing. From it is the saying of the poet:
"As if a jar from the house of Ra's, as if its blend were honey and water."
And the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:
"You turned the cup away from us, Umm ʿAmr, while the cup used to run to us on the right."
"Aged, as if the herbs in it, when water mixes with it, were heated."
From it comes the "mizaj" of the body, which is what is mixed into it of humours. As for "al-kafur," it was said: it is the name of a spring in Paradise called "al-Kafuri," by whose water the wine of Paradise is blended.
Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is blended for them with camphor, and sealed for them with musk.
ʿIkrimah said: its "mizaj" is its taste. It was also said that the camphor is only in its scent, not in its taste.

It was also said that he meant camphor in its whiteness, the fineness of its fragrance, and its coolness, because camphor is not drunk, as in His saying: ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "as fire."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Musk, camphor and ginger perfumed it."

Muqatil said: "It is not the camphor of this world. God named what is with Him by what is with you so that hearts may be guided to it." The clause is in the position of a genitive qualifier (sifah) for "a cup."

It was also said that "kana" (was) here is redundant, meaning: "from a cup whose mixture is camphor."

﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾: ʿaynan (a spring) is in the accusative because it is a badal (substitute) for kafuran (camphor), since its water is as white as camphor.

Makki said: it is a badal from the position of "min kas" (from a cup), with an omitted mudaf (qualified noun), as if it were said: "They drink a wine whose wine is of a spring." It was also said that it is accusative as the object of "yashrabun" (they drink), meaning "a spring from a cup." It was also said that it is accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), as al-Akhfash said. It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb explained by what follows, meaning: "They drink a spring from which the servants of God drink." The first view is the better one, and the clause ﴿from which the servants of God drink﴾ is a qualifier of ʿaynan.

It was also said that the preposition (ba') in ﴿drink from it﴾ is redundant. It was also said that it means "min" (from), as al-Zajjaj said, and the reading of Ibn Abi ʿAbla supports this: "yashrabuha ʿibadu Allah" (the servants of God drink it).

It was also said that "yashrabu" (drink) is taken to include the sense of "yaltadhdhu" (delight in), and it was also said that the phrase is connected to "yashrabu," with the pronoun referring back to the cup.

Al-Farra' said: "yashrabuha" and "yashrabu biha" are the same in meaning, and it seems that "yashrabu biha" means "they are quenched by it and benefit from it." He recited the verse of al-Hudhali:

"They drank with sea water, then they rose up."

He said: "Similar to it is: 'He spoke with a good speech' and 'He spoke a good speech.'"

﴿They make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾: meaning they lead it wherever they wish and benefit from it as they please, and its water follows them to every place they want it to reach. They split it, as a river is split and made to gush here and there.

Mujahid said: "They lead it wherever they wish, and it follows them wherever they turn; it turns with them." This clause is another qualifier of ʿaynan.

﴿They fulfil their vows﴾: this clause is a new sentence (isti'naf) that explains the reason for which they were given what was mentioned, and so is what is conjoined to it. The meaning of "nadhr" (vow) linguistically is obligation, and the meaning is: they fulfil what God has made obligatory upon them of acts of obedience.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: they fulfil the obedience of God, such as prayer, pilgrimage and the like.

Ikrimah said: they fulfil when they vow in the right of God, glorified is He. In the Shari'ah, a vow is what a responsible person makes obligatory upon himself, so the meaning is: they fulfil what they have made obligatory upon themselves.

Al-Farra' said: there is an implied element in the speech, meaning: they used to fulfil vows in the world.

Al-Kalbi said: "They fulfil the covenant," meaning they complete the covenant.

The better reading of "vow" here is what the servant makes obligatory upon himself, without restriction.

﴿And they fear a day whose evil will be widespread﴾: the intended day is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of its evil being "istitarah" (spreading) is its being widespread and dispersed. It is said: "istatara yastiru istitarah, fahuwa mustatir," and it is the form "istaf'ala" from "tayaran" (flying). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She spent the night, having stirred in the heart a crack, despite her distance, spreading."

The Arabs say: "The crack spread in the flask or the bottle" when it extends, and it is said: "al-harig istatar" (the fire spread) when it spreads.

Al-Farra' said: "al-mustatir" means "al-mustatil" (extended).

Qatadah said: the evil of that day spread until it filled the heavens and the earth.

Muqatil said: its evil was pervasive in the heavens, so they were split, the stars were scattered, and the angels were terrified; and on earth the mountains were blown away and the waters sank.

﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive﴾: meaning they feed these three categories the food, despite their love for it and its scarcity among them.

Mujahid said: "Despite its scarcity, their love for it and their desire for it." So His saying "ʿala hubbihi" (in spite of their love for it) is in the accusative position as a hal (circumstantial clause), meaning: they, while loving it. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92]. It was also said: "in spite of love of giving food, out of their eagerness for good." Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: "In spite of love of giving food."

It was also said that the pronoun in "hubbihi" refers to God: meaning they give food, giving it out of love for God; that is, they give food out of love of God.

This is supported by His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾.

The miskin (needy) is one in misery (maskanah), who is poor, or one who is poorer than the poor. By the orphan is meant the orphans of the Muslims. The captive is one who is taken captive and then confined.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: the captive is the one confined.

Ikrimah said: the captive is the slave.

Abu Hamzah al-Thumali said: the captive is the woman.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the verse of charity (sadaqat) and the verse of the sword abrogated (naskh) this feeding concerning the captive who is a disbeliever. Others said: rather, it is muhkam (not abrogated), and feeding the needy and the orphan is voluntary, while feeding the captive is to preserve his life until the ruler decides concerning him.

The clause ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾ is in the accusative position as a hal, with an implied verb of saying: meaning they say, "We only feed you," or they are saying, "We only feed you." This means that they do not expect repayment and do not want the people's praise for it, nor do they seek to be completed by it through this; but God knew it from their hearts and praised them for it.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: they did not say this, but God knew it from their hearts and praised them, and from His praise it is known that they did this [p. 1565] out of fear of God and hope for His reward.

﴿We do not want from you any reward or thanks﴾: meaning we do not seek from you repayment for this feeding, nor do we want thanks from you to us; rather it is purely for the sake of God. This sentence confirms what precedes it, because whoever feeds for the sake of God does not want repayment and does not seek thanks from the one he feeds.

﴿Indeed we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾: meaning we fear the punishment of a day characterised by these two qualities. The meaning of "ʿabusan" (austere) is that it is a day on which faces frown from its terror and severity, so the meaning is: it has frowning.

Al-Farra', Abu ʿUbayda and al-Mubarrad said: "yawman qamtariran" and "qumatir" are used when it is difficult and severe. Al-Farra' recited:

"Sons of our paternal uncle, do you remember our trial against you on the day of Qumatir?"

Al-Akhfash said: "al-qamtarir" is the most intense and longest of days in trial. From this is the saying of the poet:

"So flee when the war has raised its dust, and the austere, qumatir day has persisted in it."

Al-Kisa'i said: "iqmatarra al-yawm wa izmaharra" means when the day is difficult and severe. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Sons of war, we bequeathed to them a qamtarah, and whoever meets from us on that day will flee."

Mujahid said: "The frowning is with the two lips, and the qitmir is with the forehead and the eyebrows," so he made them attributes of one changed on that day because of what he sees of the hardships. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"He is able to hunt with a broken stick, and he is contracted for an hour and frowning."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "Qamtarir" means contracted between the two eyes and the eyebrows.

Al-Zajjaj said: "iqmatarrat al-naqah" is said when the she-camel raises her tail, gathers her two teats, and throws out with her nose what the drops of milk precede; and he took the mim to be an added letter.

﴿So God protected them from the evil of that day﴾: meaning He gave them, instead of the frowning which the disbelievers have, brightness in the faces and joy in the hearts.

Al-Dahhak said: "Nadrah" is whiteness and purity in their faces.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is beauty and radiance. It was also said: nadrah is the trace of blessing.

﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured﴾: meaning because of their patience in the obligations. It was also said: patience in poverty; it was also said: patience in hunger; it was also said: patience in fasting.

The better reading of the verse is that it refers to patience in everything in which patience is an act of obedience to God, glorified is He. "Ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and the implied meaning is: "for their patience." ﴿A garden and silk﴾: meaning He caused them to enter the Garden and clothed them in silk, which is the clothing of the people of the Garden, in place of leaving it in this world in compliance with what came in the Shari'ah concerning its prohibition.

The apparent generality of these verses covers everyone who fears the Day of Resurrection, feeds for the sake of God, and fears His punishment. Although the cause (sabab) is specific, as will come, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, and the cause of revelation enters under its generality as a primary entry.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man﴾: he said: "Every man."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: "amshaj" (mingled), he said: "Its amshaj are its veins."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim related: "amshaj," he said: "the veins."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿from a drop of mingled fluid﴾, he said: "The fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman when they mix."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "amshaj" means colours: the man's drop is white and red, and the woman's drop is green and red.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, he said: "al-amshaj is what comes out after urine like pieces of strings, and from it the child is formed."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, concerning His saying: "and a captive," he said: "He is the polytheist."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning His saying: 'a needy one' he said: 'poor'; 'an orphan' he said: 'one without a father'; 'a captive' he said: 'the slave and the prisoner.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿And they give food﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: "This verse was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿a day austere﴾, he said: "Narrow." "Qamtarir," he said: "long."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas ibn Malik, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying: ﴿a day austere and distressing﴾, he said: 'It contracts what is between the eyes.'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Qamtarir is the man contracted between his two eyes and his face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: ﴿And He gave them brightness and joy﴾, he said: "Brightness in their faces and joy in their breasts."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 76, verses 1–12 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: it is Madani.
Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it is Makki.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. It was also said that the part of it from His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages﴾, to the end of the surah, is Makki, and what precedes it is Madani.
Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "A man from Abyssinia came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Ask and inquire.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have been given preference over us in colours, forms and prophethood. Tell me, if I believe in what you believe in and act by what you act by, shall I be with you in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes, by Him in whose hand my soul is, indeed the whiteness of the black man will be seen in Paradise from a distance of a thousand years.' Then he said: 'Whoever says, "There is no god but Allah," has a covenant with Allah; and whoever says, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," there will be written for him one hundred thousand and twenty-four thousand good deeds.' And this surah was revealed: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾ up to His saying ﴿and a great kingdom﴾. The Abyssinian said: 'And will my eye see what your eyes see in Paradise?' He said: 'Yes.' Then he suffered until his soul departed. Ibn ʿUmar said: 'Indeed I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lower him into his grave with his own hand.'"
Ahmad in al-Zuhd narrated from Muhammad ibn Mutarrif, who said: "The trustworthy one narrated to me that a black man used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about tasbih and tahlil. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to him: 'You have asked the Messenger of Allah too much.' He said: 'Mah, O ʿUmar!' And upon the Prophet (ﷺ) was revealed ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾, until when it reached the mention of Paradise, the black man sighed a sigh and his soul departed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'He died out of longing for Paradise.'"
Ibn Wahb narrated something similar from Ibn Zayd, as a mursal marfu" report.
Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Munayʿ, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Diya' narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ until he finished it, then said: 'Indeed I see what you do not see and hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has a right to creak; there is not a space of four fingers in it but an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah. By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not enjoy women on beds, and you would go out to the high roads, crying out to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.'"

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes and the scholars of meanings that "hal" here means "qad" and is not an interrogative. Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu ʿUbaydah said this.
Al-Farra' said: "Hal" can be a negation and can be a statement; this is from the statement form, because you say: "Hal a'taytuka?" (Have I not given you?), affirming that you gave him. Negation is when you say: "Hal yaqdiru ahadun ʿala mithl hadha?" (Can anyone do the like of this?). It was also said that although it means "qad," it contains the sense of interrogation. The original is "a-hal atā," so the meaning is "a-qad atā," and the interrogation is for confirmation and approximation. The intended "insan" here is Adam, according to Qatadah, al-Thawri, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi and others. ﴿A period of time﴾: it was said it is forty years before the spirit was breathed into him. It was also said that he was created from clay for forty years, then from black mud shaped (ḥama' masnun) for forty years, then from dry clay (ṣalṣal) for forty years, so his creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years.
It was also said that the "ḥin" mentioned here has no known measure. It was said the intended "insan" is the children of Adam, and "ḥin" is the period of gestation. The clause ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from "insan," or in a position of nominative as an attribute of "ḥin."
Al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab said: the meaning is that he was a formed body of dirt and clay, not mentioned, not known, and not known what his name was or what was meant by him; then the spirit was breathed into him and he became something mentioned.
Yahya ibn Salam said: ﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ in creation, though he was a thing worth mentioning with Allah. It was also said that the intended "dhikr" here is not informing, for Allah's informing about creatures is eternal; rather it is "dhikr" in the sense of standing and nobility, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾.
Al-Qushayri said: he was not mentioned to creation, though he was mentioned to Allah, glory be to Him.
Al-Farra' said: he was a thing but was not mentioned.
Thus the negation was directed to the restriction.
It was also said the meaning is: periods of time have passed, and Adam was not a thing, nor created, nor mentioned to anyone of the creation.
Muqatil said: there is preceding and following in the speech, and its estimation is: "Has there come upon man a period of time in which he was not a thing worth mentioning?" because He created him after creating all living beings and did not create any living being after him.
﴿Indeed We created man from a drop of fluid﴾: the intended "insan" here is the son of Adam.
Al-Qurtubi said: without disagreement. The nutfah is the water that drips, which is semen, and every small amount of water in a vessel is a nutfah; its plural is nutaf. "Amshaj" is an attribute of "nutfah," and it is the plural of mashij or mashij, meaning mixtures. The intended meaning is the male's nutfah and the female's nutfah and their mixing.
It is said: "masha/a hadha bi-hadha fa-huwa mamshuj," meaning this was mixed with that, so it is mixed.
Al-Mubarrad said: "masha yamshu," when it mixes; here it is the mixing of the nutfah with blood.
Ru'bah ibn al-ʿAjjaj said:
"They cast every premature, mixed one, which has not been clothed with skin of mixed blood."
Al-Farra' said: "amshaj" is the mixing of the man's water, the woman's water, the blood and the clot. It is said "masha hadha" when he mixed. It was also said that "amshaj" is redness in whiteness and whiteness in redness. Al-Qurtubi said: this is an opinion that many lexicographers prefer.
Al-Hudhali said:
"As if the feathers and the sinew of it were the binding of the blade, tied to it with a mashij."
That is because the man's water is white and thick, and the woman's water is yellow and thin, and the child is created from both.
Ibn al-Sikkit said: "al-amshaj" are the mixtures, because they are blended from kinds from which man is created and from differing natures.
It was also said that "amshaj" is a singular word like "birmat a'shar," and this is supported by its occurrence as an adjective of "nutfah." The clause ﴿We test him﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "khalaqna," that is, intending to test him; and it may be a circumstantial clause from "insan," meaning: We test him with good and evil and with obligations.
Al-Farra' said: its meaning, and Allah knows best, is ﴿so We made him hearing and seeing﴾; "nabtalihi" is a preceding clause whose meaning is delayed, because testing does not occur except after the completion of creation, and on this view this circumstance is presumed (muqaddarah); it was also said it is concurrent (muqarinah).
It was also said the meaning of testing is transferring him from one state to another, in the manner of metaphor, but the first is preferable.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that He gave him what makes testing valid, saying: ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful﴾; that is, We made clear to him and made him know the path of guidance and misguidance, and good and evil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. Mujahid said: that is, We made clear the way to misery and happiness.
Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: the "sabil" here is his coming out of the womb. It was also said it is its benefits and harms by which he is guided by his nature and perfect intellect. The accusatives "shakiran" and "kafuran" are circumstantial from the object of "hadaynahu": that is, We enabled him to travel the path in both of his states together. It was also said they are circumstantial from "sabil" metaphorically: that is, We made the way known to him, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way.
Makki related from the Kufans that "imma" here is conditional "in" with "ma" added after it: that is, We made the way clear to him, if he is grateful and if he is ungrateful.
Al-Farra' chose this, but the Basrans do not permit it, because the conditional "in" does not enter upon nouns except when a verb is implied after it, and it is not valid here to imply a verb, because then "shakiran" and "kafuran" would have to be nominative.
It is possible to imply a verb that governs "shakiran" and "kafuran," its estimation being: if We created him grateful, then he is grateful; and if We created him disbelieving, then he is disbelieving. This is according to the reading of the majority, ﴿imma shakiran wa-imma kafuran﴾, with the hamza of "imma" kasra.
Abu al-Simak and Abu al-ʿAjjaj read it with fatha. On the fatha reading, "imma" is the coordinating particle in the dialect of some Arabs, or it is the detailing "imma," whose answer is implied. It was also said "shakiran" and "kafuran" are accusative by implying "kana," the estimation being: whether he was grateful or he was ungrateful.
Then He, glory be to Him, explained what He prepared for the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Indeed We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blaze﴾. Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, and Hisham from Ibn ʿAmir read "salasila" with tanwin; Qunbul, on stopping, from Ibn Kathir, and Hamzah stopped without alif; and the rest stopped with alif.
The reasoning of those who read "salasila" with tanwin, despite its having the form of the diptote plurals, is that they intended harmony, because what precedes it, ﴿imma shakiran wa-imma kafuran﴾, and what follows it, "aghlalan wa-sa'iran," are tanwined; or it is according to the dialect of those who make all diptotes triptote, as al-Kisa'i and others of the Kufans related from some Arabs.
Al-Akhfash said: we have heard from the Arabs one who makes triptote every diptote, because the original in nouns is triptote, and the non-triptote is left out due to an accidental factor in them.
Al-Farra' said: it is according to the dialect of those who put all nouns in the genitive, except the saying "hu azrafu minka" (he is more refined than you), for they do not put it in the genitive. Ibn al-Anbari cited in this regard the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:
"As if our swords among us and among them were batons in the hands of players."
From it is the saying of a poet:
"And when the men see Yazid, you see them, humbled of necks, lowering of gazes."
With a kasra on the sin of "nawakis." And the saying of Labid:
"And the hard-worn curtains, they call upon her for her doom, with fastenings whose hooks are similar."
And also his saying:
"Bounty, and one of generosity who helps toward liberality, gracious, mixing with the desires of its flocks."
It was also said that the tanwin is for agreement with the orthography of the Makki, Madani and Kufan codices, for they have it with an alif. It was also said that this tanwin is a substitute for the vowel of pausal lengthening (harf al-itlaq), and the connected reading runs like the pause. "Salasil" has already been explained, and the difference concerning it is whether they are the fetters, or what is placed on the necks, as in the saying of the poet:
". . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
But the chains and the shackles have encircled the necks."
"Aghlal" is the plural of "ghull," by which hands are bound to the necks. "Sa'ir" is intense fuel, and the explanation of "sa'ir" has already preceded.
Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what He prepared for the grateful, saying: ﴿Indeed the righteous will drink from a cup﴾. "Al-abrar" are the people of obedience and sincerity; "al-sadq" is the plural of barr or barir.
Al-Sihah says: the plural of "al-barr" is "al-abrar," and the plural of "al-barr" (the dutiful one) is "al-barara," and it is said: "fulan yabarru khaliqahu wa-yabrurahu," that is, he obeys Him.
Al-Hasan said: "al-barr" is one who does not harm even an ant.
Qatadah said: "al-abrar" are those who fulfill Allah's right and keep their vows.
(p-1564) The "ka's" in the language is the vessel in which there is drink; if there is no drink in it, it is not called a "ka's." There is no basis for restricting it to glass; rather it may be of glass, of gold, of silver, of porcelain and other things, and the cups of the Arabs were of different kinds. The word "ka's" may also be applied to the wine itself, as in the saying of the poet:
"And a cup I drank with pleasure, and another by which I treated myself."
﴿Its mixture will be camphor﴾: that is, it is mixed with it and blended with it. It is said "mazajahu yamzujuhu mazjan," that is, he mixed it, he mixes it, mixing. From it is the saying of the poet:
"As if a jar from the house of Ra's, as if its blend were honey and water."
And the saying of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:
"You turned the cup away from us, Umm ʿAmr, while the cup used to run to us on the right."
"Aged, as if the herbs in it, when water mixes with it, were heated."
From it comes the "mizaj" of the body, which is what is mixed into it of humours. As for "al-kafur," it was said: it is the name of a spring in Paradise called "al-Kafuri," by whose water the wine of Paradise is blended.
Qatadah and Mujahid said: it is blended for them with camphor, and sealed for them with musk.
ʿIkrimah said: its "mizaj" is its taste. It was also said that the camphor is only in its scent, not in its taste.

It was also said that he meant camphor in its whiteness, the fineness of its fragrance, and its coolness, because camphor is not drunk, as in His saying: ﴿until, when he had made it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], meaning "as fire."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Musk, camphor and ginger perfumed it."

Muqatil said: "It is not the camphor of this world. God named what is with Him by what is with you so that hearts may be guided to it." The clause is in the position of a genitive qualifier (sifah) for "a cup."

It was also said that "kana" (was) here is redundant, meaning: "from a cup whose mixture is camphor."

﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾: ʿaynan (a spring) is in the accusative because it is a badal (substitute) for kafuran (camphor), since its water is as white as camphor.

Makki said: it is a badal from the position of "min kas" (from a cup), with an omitted mudaf (qualified noun), as if it were said: "They drink a wine whose wine is of a spring." It was also said that it is accusative as the object of "yashrabun" (they drink), meaning "a spring from a cup." It was also said that it is accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), as al-Akhfash said. It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb explained by what follows, meaning: "They drink a spring from which the servants of God drink." The first view is the better one, and the clause ﴿from which the servants of God drink﴾ is a qualifier of ʿaynan.

It was also said that the preposition (ba') in ﴿drink from it﴾ is redundant. It was also said that it means "min" (from), as al-Zajjaj said, and the reading of Ibn Abi ʿAbla supports this: "yashrabuha ʿibadu Allah" (the servants of God drink it).

It was also said that "yashrabu" (drink) is taken to include the sense of "yaltadhdhu" (delight in), and it was also said that the phrase is connected to "yashrabu," with the pronoun referring back to the cup.

Al-Farra' said: "yashrabuha" and "yashrabu biha" are the same in meaning, and it seems that "yashrabu biha" means "they are quenched by it and benefit from it." He recited the verse of al-Hudhali:

"They drank with sea water, then they rose up."

He said: "Similar to it is: 'He spoke with a good speech' and 'He spoke a good speech.'"

﴿They make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾: meaning they lead it wherever they wish and benefit from it as they please, and its water follows them to every place they want it to reach. They split it, as a river is split and made to gush here and there.

Mujahid said: "They lead it wherever they wish, and it follows them wherever they turn; it turns with them." This clause is another qualifier of ʿaynan.

﴿They fulfil their vows﴾: this clause is a new sentence (isti'naf) that explains the reason for which they were given what was mentioned, and so is what is conjoined to it. The meaning of "nadhr" (vow) linguistically is obligation, and the meaning is: they fulfil what God has made obligatory upon them of acts of obedience.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: they fulfil the obedience of God, such as prayer, pilgrimage and the like.

Ikrimah said: they fulfil when they vow in the right of God, glorified is He. In the Shari'ah, a vow is what a responsible person makes obligatory upon himself, so the meaning is: they fulfil what they have made obligatory upon themselves.

Al-Farra' said: there is an implied element in the speech, meaning: they used to fulfil vows in the world.

Al-Kalbi said: "They fulfil the covenant," meaning they complete the covenant.

The better reading of "vow" here is what the servant makes obligatory upon himself, without restriction.

﴿And they fear a day whose evil will be widespread﴾: the intended day is the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of its evil being "istitarah" (spreading) is its being widespread and dispersed. It is said: "istatara yastiru istitarah, fahuwa mustatir," and it is the form "istaf'ala" from "tayaran" (flying). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"She spent the night, having stirred in the heart a crack, despite her distance, spreading."

The Arabs say: "The crack spread in the flask or the bottle" when it extends, and it is said: "al-harig istatar" (the fire spread) when it spreads.

Al-Farra' said: "al-mustatir" means "al-mustatil" (extended).

Qatadah said: the evil of that day spread until it filled the heavens and the earth.

Muqatil said: its evil was pervasive in the heavens, so they were split, the stars were scattered, and the angels were terrified; and on earth the mountains were blown away and the waters sank.

﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive﴾: meaning they feed these three categories the food, despite their love for it and its scarcity among them.

Mujahid said: "Despite its scarcity, their love for it and their desire for it." So His saying "ʿala hubbihi" (in spite of their love for it) is in the accusative position as a hal (circumstantial clause), meaning: they, while loving it. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92]. It was also said: "in spite of love of giving food, out of their eagerness for good." Al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad said: "In spite of love of giving food."

It was also said that the pronoun in "hubbihi" refers to God: meaning they give food, giving it out of love for God; that is, they give food out of love of God.

This is supported by His saying: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾.

The miskin (needy) is one in misery (maskanah), who is poor, or one who is poorer than the poor. By the orphan is meant the orphans of the Muslims. The captive is one who is taken captive and then confined.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: the captive is the one confined.

Ikrimah said: the captive is the slave.

Abu Hamzah al-Thumali said: the captive is the woman.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the verse of charity (sadaqat) and the verse of the sword abrogated (naskh) this feeding concerning the captive who is a disbeliever. Others said: rather, it is muhkam (not abrogated), and feeding the needy and the orphan is voluntary, while feeding the captive is to preserve his life until the ruler decides concerning him.

The clause ﴿We feed you only for the sake of God﴾ is in the accusative position as a hal, with an implied verb of saying: meaning they say, "We only feed you," or they are saying, "We only feed you." This means that they do not expect repayment and do not want the people's praise for it, nor do they seek to be completed by it through this; but God knew it from their hearts and praised them for it.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: they did not say this, but God knew it from their hearts and praised them, and from His praise it is known that they did this [p. 1565] out of fear of God and hope for His reward.

﴿We do not want from you any reward or thanks﴾: meaning we do not seek from you repayment for this feeding, nor do we want thanks from you to us; rather it is purely for the sake of God. This sentence confirms what precedes it, because whoever feeds for the sake of God does not want repayment and does not seek thanks from the one he feeds.

﴿Indeed we fear from our Lord a day austere and distressing﴾: meaning we fear the punishment of a day characterised by these two qualities. The meaning of "ʿabusan" (austere) is that it is a day on which faces frown from its terror and severity, so the meaning is: it has frowning.

Al-Farra', Abu ʿUbayda and al-Mubarrad said: "yawman qamtariran" and "qumatir" are used when it is difficult and severe. Al-Farra' recited:

"Sons of our paternal uncle, do you remember our trial against you on the day of Qumatir?"

Al-Akhfash said: "al-qamtarir" is the most intense and longest of days in trial. From this is the saying of the poet:

"So flee when the war has raised its dust, and the austere, qumatir day has persisted in it."

Al-Kisa'i said: "iqmatarra al-yawm wa izmaharra" means when the day is difficult and severe. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Sons of war, we bequeathed to them a qamtarah, and whoever meets from us on that day will flee."

Mujahid said: "The frowning is with the two lips, and the qitmir is with the forehead and the eyebrows," so he made them attributes of one changed on that day because of what he sees of the hardships. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"He is able to hunt with a broken stick, and he is contracted for an hour and frowning."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "Qamtarir" means contracted between the two eyes and the eyebrows.

Al-Zajjaj said: "iqmatarrat al-naqah" is said when the she-camel raises her tail, gathers her two teats, and throws out with her nose what the drops of milk precede; and he took the mim to be an added letter.

﴿So God protected them from the evil of that day﴾: meaning He gave them, instead of the frowning which the disbelievers have, brightness in the faces and joy in the hearts.

Al-Dahhak said: "Nadrah" is whiteness and purity in their faces.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is beauty and radiance. It was also said: nadrah is the trace of blessing.

﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured﴾: meaning because of their patience in the obligations. It was also said: patience in poverty; it was also said: patience in hunger; it was also said: patience in fasting.

The better reading of the verse is that it refers to patience in everything in which patience is an act of obedience to God, glorified is He. "Ma" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and the implied meaning is: "for their patience." ﴿A garden and silk﴾: meaning He caused them to enter the Garden and clothed them in silk, which is the clothing of the people of the Garden, in place of leaving it in this world in compliance with what came in the Shari'ah concerning its prohibition.

The apparent generality of these verses covers everyone who fears the Day of Resurrection, feeds for the sake of God, and fears His punishment. Although the cause (sabab) is specific, as will come, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, and the cause of revelation enters under its generality as a primary entry.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿Has there come upon man﴾: he said: "Every man."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: "amshaj" (mingled), he said: "Its amshaj are its veins."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim related: "amshaj," he said: "the veins."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿from a drop of mingled fluid﴾, he said: "The fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman when they mix."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "amshaj" means colours: the man's drop is white and red, and the woman's drop is green and red.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, he said: "al-amshaj is what comes out after urine like pieces of strings, and from it the child is formed."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, concerning His saying: "and a captive," he said: "He is the polytheist."

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning His saying: 'a needy one' he said: 'poor'; 'an orphan' he said: 'one without a father'; 'a captive' he said: 'the slave and the prisoner.'"

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿And they give food﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: "This verse was revealed concerning ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿a day austere﴾, he said: "Narrow." "Qamtarir," he said: "long."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas ibn Malik, "from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying: ﴿a day austere and distressing﴾, he said: 'It contracts what is between the eyes.'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Qamtarir is the man contracted between his two eyes and his face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: ﴿And He gave them brightness and joy﴾, he said: "Brightness in their faces and joy in their breasts."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 76, verses 1–12 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: it is Madani.
Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: it is Makki.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed in Makkah.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. It was also said that the part of it from His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in stages﴾, to the end of the surah, is Makki, and what precedes it is Madani.
