Mujāhid and others said: they brought it according to their measure of satisfaction, without excess or deficiency.

Al-Kalbī said: That is more delicious and more appetizing. It was also said: the angels measured it. It was also said: the people of Paradise, the drinkers, measured it according to the measure of their desires and needs, so it came as they wanted in form, neither exceeding nor falling short.

ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sulamī, al-Sha'bī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Abū ʿAmr in one narration from him read (quddirūhā) with a ḍammah on the qāf and a kasrah on the dāl, in the passive voice: i.e. it was made for them according to their desire.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: This is of the type of inversion (qalb). He said: because the real meaning is that it should be said: "it was measured for them", not "they measured it", since it has the meaning of "they were measured for it."

Abū Ḥātim said: The measure: the vessels were measured according to the measure of their satisfaction, so the object of the passive, its subject, is omitted.

Abū Ḥayyān said: The closer explanation for the derivation of this irregular reading is to say: "their satisfaction was measured from it, a measure", so the genitive noun is omitted and it became (quddirū hā).

Al-Mahdawī said: the meaning of the last reading returns to the meaning of the first reading, and it seems that the original was (qadarū 'alayhā), then the prepositional particle was omitted, as Sībawayh recited:

"I swore I would not eat the love of Iraq as long as the years last, and love in the village is eaten by the weevil."

That is: "I swore upon the love of Iraq."

﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: it has already been stated that the cup is the vessel that contains wine, and if it is empty of wine it is not called a cup. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will be given to drink in Paradise a cup of wine mixed with ginger, and the Arabs used to enjoy mixing drink with ginger for the pleasantness of its fragrance.

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: Zanjabīl is the name of a spring from which those brought near (al-muqarrabūn) drink.

Muqātil said: It is ginger, but not like the ginger of this world.

﴿A spring therein named Salsabīl﴾: the accusative of (ʿaynan, "a spring") is that it is an apposition (badal) from (kaʾsan, "a cup"). It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by an omitted verb: i.e. "they are given to drink a spring." It is permissible that it be in the accusative by removal of the preposition: i.e. "from a spring." Al-salsabīl is the delicious drink, derived from al-salāsah (smoothness). The Arabs say: "this is a smooth drink (sharāb salis)", and "salsāl" and "salsabīl", i.e. good and delicious.

Al-Zajjāj said: Salsabīl in the language is the name of water in extreme smoothness, sharp in its flow, which goes down easily in their throats. From this is the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

"They are given to drink from the flow of al-Barīṣ over them, a cup that clinks with the smooth, sealed wine (al-raḥīq al-salsal)."

﴿And there will go around them youths made eternal﴾: when He, glory be to Him, finished describing their drink, and the description of their vessels, and the description of the servers who give them that drink.

The meaning of (mukhalladūn, "made eternal") is that they remain as they are in youth, freshness, and radiance, not aging nor changing. It was also said: the meaning of mukhalladūn is that they do not die. It was also said: takhlīd means adornment, i.e. they are adorned.

﴿When you see them, you think them scattered pearls﴾: when you look at them, you suppose them, because of their great beauty, the clarity of their colors, and the brightness of their faces, scattered pearls, unstrung.

ʿAṭāʾ said: He means in whiteness of color and its beauty, and pearls when scattered from the string on a carpet are finer than when strung.

The people of meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: They were only compared to scattered pearls because they scatter about in service, and if they were in rows they would have been compared to strung pearls. It was also said: He compared them to scattered pearls because they are swift in service, unlike the dark-eyed houris, for He compared them to hidden pearls, because they are not degraded by service.

﴿And when you look there, you see bliss and a great dominion﴾: i.e. and when you cast your sight there, meaning in the Garden, you see bliss that cannot be described, and a great dominion whose measure cannot be estimated. (Thamma, "there") is a noun of place, and its governing element is (ra'ayta, "you see").

Al-Farrā' said: in the speech there is an implied (mā), i.e. "and when you see what is there", like His saying: ﴿Surely your connection has been cut﴾ [al-An'ām: 94], i.e. what is between you.

Al-Zajjāj objected to al-Farrā', saying: it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave out the relative clause, but (ra'ayta) transitively reaches (thamma) in meaning. The meaning is: "when you see with your sight there", and by (thamma) he means the Garden.

Al-Suddī said: bliss is what one enjoys, and the great dominion is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. Muqātil and al-Kalbī said the same.

It was also said that (ra'ayta) has no object, neither spoken, nor implied, nor intended; rather its meaning is: wherever your sight falls in the Garden, you see bliss and a great dominion.

﴿Above them are garments of green silk﴾: Nāfi', Ḥamzah, and Ibn Muḥaysin read (ʿāliyahum) with a sukūn on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ, as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and (thiyāb, "garments") as a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), or (ʿāliyahum) is a subject (mubtada'), and (thiyāb) is in the nominative as the agent of the attribute, even though the attribute does not depend on a preceding element, as is the view of al-Akhfash.

Al-Farrā' said: It is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (thiyāb sundus), and the active participle is meant as a plural.

The rest read with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the hāʾ, as an adverbial of place (ẓarf) in the nominative position as a predicate placed first, and (thiyāb) as a postponed subject, as if it had been said: "above them are garments."

Al-Farrā' said: (ʿāliyahum) means "above them", and so said Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.

Abū Ḥayyān said: ʿālin and ʿāliyah are active participles, so for them to be adverbs of place they would need to be transmitted from the speech of the Arabs. Al-Zajjāj had already preceded him in this and said: "This is something we do not know in adverbs. Had it been an adverb, why would it not be permissible to make the yāʾ quiescent?" Rather it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of two things: the first is the hāʾ and mīm in His saying ﴿circulate among them﴾, i.e. around the righteous, (wildān, "youths") are high above the righteous, (thiyāb sundus, "garments of green silk"), i.e. they go around them in this state.

The second is that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the youths: i.e. when you see them you suppose them scattered pearls while the garments are above their bodies.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the governing element of the circumstantial qualifier is either (laqqāhum naḍratan wa-surūran, "He gave them radiance and joy") or (jazāhum bi-mā ṣabarū, "He rewarded them for what they endured"). He said: it is also permissible that it be an adverb of place.

Ibn Sīrīn, Mujāhid, Abū Ḥaywah, and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read ʿalayhim, "over them", a reading clear in meaning and evident in indication.

Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, because of the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: ʿāliyatuhum.

The majority read (thiyāb, "garments") with an annexation to (sundus).

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read (thiyābun) with tanwīn and cutting it off from the annexation, and (sundusun) in the nominative. And (khuḍrun wa-istabraq, "green and brocade") are: the sundus is an attribute of the garments, because sundus is a kind of garment; and (khuḍr) is an attribute of sundus, because it may be green and not green; and (istabraq) is coordinated with sundus, i.e. "and garments of brocade."

The majority of readers differed over ﴿green and brocade﴾, while agreeing on the genitive of sundus through the annexation of (thiyāb) to it. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Muḥaysin read (khuḍrin) in the genitive as an attribute of (sundus), and (istabraqu) in the nominative, coordinated with (thiyāb): i.e. "upon them are garments of sundus, and upon them is brocade."

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read (khuḍarun) in the nominative as an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqin) in the genitive as an attribute of sundus.

Abū Ḥātim and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this reading, because (khuḍr) is best when it is an attribute of garments, so it is in the nominative, and brocade is of the same kind as sundus.

Nāfi' and Ḥafṣ read ﴿green and brocade﴾ in the nominative, because (khuḍrun) is an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqun) is coordinated with (thiyāb).

Al-Farra' and Abu Qilaba... Let me produce the translation.

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "khudrin wa-istabraqin" with the genitive (jarr), taking "khudrin" as an adjective (na't) of "sundus" and "istabraqin" as conjoined (ma'tuf) to "sundus."

All of them read "istabraqin" with tanwin (ṣarf), except Ibn Muhaysin, who did not give it tanwin. He said: "Because it is a foreign (a'jami) word." There is no basis for this, because it is indefinite (nakira), unless he means that it is a proper name ( 'alam) for this kind of garment.

Al-sundus (fine silk brocade) is what is thin of ad-dibaj (silk brocade). Al-istabraq is what is thick of it. Their meanings were already explained in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yatufu 'alayhim" (they will be served by youths circulating among them).

Here, He, glorified is He, mentions that they will be adorned with bracelets of silver. In Surat Fatir, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [Fatir: 33], and in Surat al-Hajj, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾ [al-Hajj: 23]. There is no contradiction between these verses, since they can be reconciled: either He gives them bracelets of gold, silver and pearls together, or the meaning is that they wear bracelets of gold at one time, bracelets of silver at another, and bracelets of pearls at another, or each person wears of them what his soul inclines to. It is also permissible for this sentence to be in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "'aliyahum," with "qad" implied.

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: this is another kind of drink with which Allah bestows favor upon them.

Al-Farra' said: It means it is pure, not impure, as it was in the world, where it was described as impure.

The meaning is that this drink is pure, unlike the wine of this world.

Muqatil said: It is a spring at the gate of the Garden; whoever drinks from it, Allah removes from his heart whatever deceit, rancor and envy it contained.

Abu Qilaba and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: They are brought food, and when it is finished they bring the pure drink, so they drink, and their stomachs become lean from it, and sweat flows from their bodies like the scent of musk.

﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward﴾: that is, it is said to them: this which has been mentioned of kinds of blessings has been for you a reward for your deeds, that is, a recompense for them. ﴿And your effort has been appreciated﴾: that is, your deeds in the world in obedience to Allah were accepted and approved. Allah's appreciation of His servant's deed is His acceptance of his obedience.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: az-zamharir is the severe cold.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Fire complained to its Lord, saying: 'My Lord, some of me has consumed others of me.' So He allowed it two breaths: a breath in summer and a breath in winter. Therefore, the intense cold you feel is from its zamharir, and the intense heat you feel in summer is from its samum."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad ibn al-Sari, Abd ibn Humayd, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib regarding His words ﴿And near them will be its shade﴾ that he said: close. ﴿And its fruit will be lowered in readiness﴾ he said: The people of the Garden eat from the fruits of the Garden standing, sitting, and reclining, and in whatever state they wish.

In another wording he said: it is made submissive, so they take from it however they wish.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "vessels of silver whose clearness is like the clearness of glass" ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾: he said: they were measured for the hand.

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen through it; but the glass of Paradise is the whiteness of silver with the clearness of glass.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also: There is nothing in Paradise except that you have been given its likeness in this world, except glass made of silver.

Al-Firyabi narrated from him also regarding His words ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾ he said: They are brought in a measure suited to the mouth; they do not prefer anything, nor desire anything after it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him also: ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾ he said: the cup-bearers determined it.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Amr who said: The lowest in rank among the people of Paradise is one whom a thousand servants attend, each servant occupied with a task which its master does not have. He recited this verse: ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾.

His saying: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the object of (jazāhum, "rewarded them"). The governing element is (jazā, "rewarded"), and "patient" (ṣabarū) does not govern it, because patience was only in this world. Abū al-Baqā' permitted that it be an attribute of (jannah, "garden").

Al-Farrā' said: If you wish, you may make (muttaki'īn, "reclining") a follower (tābi'), as if he had said: "He rewarded them with a garden, reclining therein."

Al-Akhfash said: It may be in the accusative by way of praise (madḥ), and the pronoun in (fīhā, "therein") refers to the garden. Al-arā'ik (the couches) are the thrones within canopies (ḥijāl), and their explanation has already been given in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿They see therein no sun nor freezing cold (zamharīr)﴾: the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the object of (jazāhum), so it is among the successive circumstantial qualifiers (al-ḥāl al-mutarādifah), or it is from the pronoun in (muttaki'īn), so it is among the interlocking circumstantial qualifiers (al-ḥāl al-mutadākhilah), or it is another attribute of the garden. Al-zamharīr is the most intense cold. The meaning is that they do not see in the Garden the heat of the sun nor the cold of zamharīr. From this is the saying of al-A'shā:

"Pampered, a young girl, like a gazelle; she has not seen sun nor zamharīr."

Tha'lab said: Al-zamharīr is the moon in the dialect of Ṭayyi', and he recited a verse of their poet:

"And a night whose darkness has gathered thick, I crossed it while the zamharīr had not shone."

It is also narrated as "had not appeared", meaning the moon had not risen. The explanation of this has already been given in Surat Maryam.

﴿And near over them are its shades﴾: the majority of readers read (dāniyatan, "near") in the accusative, as a coordination with the position of (lā yarawna, "they do not see"), or with (muttaki'īn), or as an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e. "and a garden near", as if he had said: "and He rewarded them with a near garden."

Al-Zajjāj said: It is an attribute of the previously mentioned "garden."

Al-Farrā' said: It is in the accusative by way of praise.

Abū Ḥaywah read (wa-dāniyatun, "and near") in the nominative, as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), with (ẓilāluhā, "its shades") as a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier.

The meaning: the shadows of the trees are close to them, shading over them, as an increase in their bliss, even though there is no sun there.

Muqātil said: It means its trees are near them.

Ibn Mas'ūd read (wa-dāniyan 'alayhim), "and near over them."

﴿Its fruit-clusters are made easy to reach, with complete ease﴾: it is coordinated with (dāniyatan), as if he had said: "and made easy (muzallalah)." It is permissible that the clause be in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ('alayhim), and it is permissible that it be a new independent sentence. Al-quṭūf are the fruits. The meaning is that its fruits have been made subservient to those who pick them, with very great subservience, such that one who stands, sits, or lies down can take them, and neither distance nor thorn turns their hands away from them.

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-mudhallal is that which is near to hand and easy to reach. From this is their saying: "a low wall" (ḥā'iṭun dhalīl), i.e. short.

Ibn Qutaybah said: dhullilat means "brought near", from their saying "a low wall", i.e. it was short in height. It was also said: dhullilat means made submissive, not resisting those who pick them however they wish.

﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and goblets﴾: i.e. servants go around them when they want drink, with vessels of silver. Al-akwāb is the plural of kūb, which is a large jug with no handle nor loop. From this is the saying of 'Adī:

"Reclining, whose doors are knocked upon, a servant serves over him with the kūb."

Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Zukhruf.

﴿Crystal-clear glass, crystal of silver﴾: i.e. in the description of the glass, in clarity and in the whiteness of silver. Its clarity is the clarity of glass, and its color is the color of silver.

Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī, and Abū Bakr read (qawārīra qawārīra) with tanwīn on both with pause and connection, and with pausing on both with an alif. The aspect of this reading has already been given in the explanation of His saying (salāsil, "chains") in this surah, and we explained there the reason for declining what has the form of the final plural pattern, so return to it.

Ḥamzah read without tanwīn on both and without pausing with an alif. The aspect of this reading is clear, since both are excluded from declension by the form of the final plural pattern.

Hishām read without tanwīn on both with pausing on both with an alif. Ibn Kathīr read with tanwīn on the first without the second, and pausing on the first with an alif without the second.

Abū 'Amr, Ḥafṣ, and Ibn Dhakwān read without tanwīn on both, and pausing on the first with an alif, not the second. The clause is in the genitive position as an attribute of (akwāb, "goblets").

Abū al-Baqā' said: The repetition is good because of what is attached to it, namely the explanation of its origin.

al-Wāḥidī said: The exegetes said: God made the glass of the people of Paradise of silver, so there combined for it the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Zajjāj said: The glass that is in this world is made of sand, and God informed us of the excellence of that glass, that its origin is silver, so that what is inside it is seen from its outside.

The clause ﴿they have measured it with measure﴾ is an attribute of (qawārīr, "glass").

The majority read (qaddarūhā, "they measured it") with a fatḥah on the qāf, in the active voice: i.e. the servers, from among the attendants who go around them, measured it according to what the drinkers of the people of Paradise need, without excess or deficiency.

Mujāhid and others said: they brought it according to their measure of satisfaction, without excess or deficiency.

Al-Kalbī said: That is more delicious and more appetizing. It was also said: the angels measured it. It was also said: the people of Paradise, the drinkers, measured it according to the measure of their desires and needs, so it came as they wanted in form, neither exceeding nor falling short.

ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sulamī, al-Sha'bī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Abū ʿAmr in one narration from him read (quddirūhā) with a ḍammah on the qāf and a kasrah on the dāl, in the passive voice: i.e. it was made for them according to their desire.

That is: "I swore upon the love of Iraq."

The rest read with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the hāʾ, as an adverbial of place (ẓarf) in the nominative position as a predicate placed first, and (thiyāb) as a postponed subject, as if it had been said: "above them are garments."

Al-Farrā' said: (ʿāliyahum) means "above them", and so said Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.

Abū Ḥayyān said: ʿālin and ʿāliyah are active participles, so for them to be adverbs of place they would need to be transmitted from the speech of the Arabs. Al-Zajjāj had already preceded him in this and said: "This is something we do not know in adverbs. Had it been an adverb, why would it not be permissible to make the yāʾ quiescent?" Rather it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of two things: the first is the hāʾ and mīm in His saying ﴿circulate among them﴾, i.e. around the righteous, (wildān, "youths") are high above the righteous, (thiyāb sundus, "garments of green silk"), i.e. they go around them in this state.

The second is that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the youths: i.e. when you see them you suppose them scattered pearls while the garments are above their bodies.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the governing element of the circumstantial qualifier is either (laqqāhum naḍratan wa-surūran, "He gave them radiance and joy") or (jazāhum bi-mā ṣabarū, "He rewarded them for what they endured"). He said: it is also permissible that it be an adverb of place.

Ibn Sīrīn, Mujāhid, Abū Ḥaywah, and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read ʿalayhim, "over them", a reading clear in meaning and evident in indication.

Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, because of the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: ʿāliyatuhum.

The majority read (thiyāb, "garments") with an annexation to (sundus).

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read (thiyābun) with tanwīn and cutting it off from the annexation, and (sundusun) in the nominative. And (khuḍrun wa-istabraq, "green and brocade") are: the sundus is an attribute of the garments, because sundus is a kind of garment; and (khuḍr) is an attribute of sundus, because it may be green and not green; and (istabraq) is coordinated with sundus, i.e. "and garments of brocade."

The majority of readers differed over ﴿green and brocade﴾, while agreeing on the genitive of sundus through the annexation of (thiyāb) to it. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Muḥaysin read (khuḍrin) in the genitive as an attribute of (sundus), and (istabraqu) in the nominative, coordinated with (thiyāb): i.e. "upon them are garments of sundus, and upon them is brocade."

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read (khuḍarun) in the nominative as an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqin) in the genitive as an attribute of sundus.

Abū Ḥātim and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this reading, because (khuḍr) is best when it is an attribute of garments, so it is in the nominative, and brocade is of the same kind as sundus.

Nāfi' and Ḥafṣ read ﴿green and brocade﴾ in the nominative, because (khuḍrun) is an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqun) is coordinated with (thiyāb).

Al-Farra' and Abu Qilaba... Let me produce the translation.

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "khudrin wa-istabraqin" with the genitive (jarr), taking "khudrin" as an adjective (na't) of "sundus" and "istabraqin" as conjoined (ma'tuf) to "sundus."

All of them read "istabraqin" with tanwin (ṣarf), except Ibn Muhaysin, who did not give it tanwin. He said: "Because it is a foreign (a'jami) word." There is no basis for this, because it is indefinite (nakira), unless he means that it is a proper name ( 'alam) for this kind of garment.

Al-sundus (fine silk brocade) is what is thin of ad-dibaj (silk brocade). Al-istabraq is what is thick of it. Their meanings were already explained in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yatufu 'alayhim" (they will be served by youths circulating among them).

Here, He, glorified is He, mentions that they will be adorned with bracelets of silver. In Surat Fatir, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [Fatir: 33], and in Surat al-Hajj, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾ [al-Hajj: 23]. There is no contradiction between these verses, since they can be reconciled: either He gives them bracelets of gold, silver and pearls together, or the meaning is that they wear bracelets of gold at one time, bracelets of silver at another, and bracelets of pearls at another, or each person wears of them what his soul inclines to. It is also permissible for this sentence to be in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "'aliyahum," with "qad" implied.

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: this is another kind of drink with which Allah bestows favor upon them.

Al-Farra' said: It means it is pure, not impure, as it was in the world, where it was described as impure.

The meaning is that this drink is pure, unlike the wine of this world.

Muqatil said: It is a spring at the gate of the Garden; whoever drinks from it, Allah removes from his heart whatever deceit, rancor and envy it contained.

Abu Qilaba and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: They are brought food, and when it is finished they bring the pure drink, so they drink, and their stomachs become lean from it, and sweat flows from their bodies like the scent of musk.

﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward﴾: that is, it is said to them: this which has been mentioned of kinds of blessings has been for you a reward for your deeds, that is, a recompense for them. ﴿And your effort has been appreciated﴾: that is, your deeds in the world in obedience to Allah were accepted and approved. Allah's appreciation of His servant's deed is His acceptance of his obedience.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: az-zamharir is the severe cold.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Fire complained to its Lord, saying: 'My Lord, some of me has consumed others of me.' So He allowed it two breaths: a breath in summer and a breath in winter. Therefore, the intense cold you feel is from its zamharir, and the intense heat you feel in summer is from its samum."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad ibn al-Sari, Abd ibn Humayd, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib regarding His words ﴿And near them will be its shade﴾ that he said: close. ﴿And its fruit will be lowered in readiness﴾ he said: The people of the Garden eat from the fruits of the Garden standing, sitting, and reclining, and in whatever state they wish.

In another wording he said: it is made submissive, so they take from it however they wish.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "vessels of silver whose clearness is like the clearness of glass" ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾: he said: they were measured for the hand.

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen through it; but the glass of Paradise is the whiteness of silver with the clearness of glass.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also: There is nothing in Paradise except that you have been given its likeness in this world, except glass made of silver.

Al-Firyabi narrated from him also regarding His words ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾ he said: They are brought in a measure suited to the mouth; they do not prefer anything, nor desire anything after it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him also: ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾ he said: the cup-bearers determined it.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Amr who said: The lowest in rank among the people of Paradise is one whom a thousand servants attend, each servant occupied with a task which its master does not have. He recited this verse: ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾.

His saying: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the object of (jazāhum, "rewarded them"). The governing element is (jazā, "rewarded"), and "patient" (ṣabarū) does not govern it, because patience was only in this world. Abū al-Baqā' permitted that it be an attribute of (jannah, "garden").

Al-Farrā' said: If you wish, you may make (muttaki'īn, "reclining") a follower (tābi'), as if he had said: "He rewarded them with a garden, reclining therein."

Al-Akhfash said: It may be in the accusative by way of praise (madḥ), and the pronoun in (fīhā, "therein") refers to the garden. Al-arā'ik (the couches) are the thrones within canopies (ḥijāl), and their explanation has already been given in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿They see therein no sun nor freezing cold (zamharīr)﴾: the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the object of (jazāhum), so it is among the successive circumstantial qualifiers (al-ḥāl al-mutarādifah), or it is from the pronoun in (muttaki'īn), so it is among the interlocking circumstantial qualifiers (al-ḥāl al-mutadākhilah), or it is another attribute of the garden. Al-zamharīr is the most intense cold. The meaning is that they do not see in the Garden the heat of the sun nor the cold of zamharīr. From this is the saying of al-A'shā:

"Pampered, a young girl, like a gazelle; she has not seen sun nor zamharīr."

Tha'lab said: Al-zamharīr is the moon in the dialect of Ṭayyi', and he recited a verse of their poet:

"And a night whose darkness has gathered thick, I crossed it while the zamharīr had not shone."

It is also narrated as "had not appeared", meaning the moon had not risen. The explanation of this has already been given in Surat Maryam.

﴿And near over them are its shades﴾: the majority of readers read (dāniyatan, "near") in the accusative, as a coordination with the position of (lā yarawna, "they do not see"), or with (muttaki'īn), or as an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e. "and a garden near", as if he had said: "and He rewarded them with a near garden."

Al-Zajjāj said: It is an attribute of the previously mentioned "garden."

Al-Farrā' said: It is in the accusative by way of praise.

Abū Ḥaywah read (wa-dāniyatun, "and near") in the nominative, as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), with (ẓilāluhā, "its shades") as a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier.

The meaning: the shadows of the trees are close to them, shading over them, as an increase in their bliss, even though there is no sun there.

Muqātil said: It means its trees are near them.

Ibn Mas'ūd read (wa-dāniyan 'alayhim), "and near over them."

﴿Its fruit-clusters are made easy to reach, with complete ease﴾: it is coordinated with (dāniyatan), as if he had said: "and made easy (muzallalah)." It is permissible that the clause be in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ('alayhim), and it is permissible that it be a new independent sentence. Al-quṭūf are the fruits. The meaning is that its fruits have been made subservient to those who pick them, with very great subservience, such that one who stands, sits, or lies down can take them, and neither distance nor thorn turns their hands away from them.

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-mudhallal is that which is near to hand and easy to reach. From this is their saying: "a low wall" (ḥā'iṭun dhalīl), i.e. short.

Ibn Qutaybah said: dhullilat means "brought near", from their saying "a low wall", i.e. it was short in height. It was also said: dhullilat means made submissive, not resisting those who pick them however they wish.

﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and goblets﴾: i.e. servants go around them when they want drink, with vessels of silver. Al-akwāb is the plural of kūb, which is a large jug with no handle nor loop. From this is the saying of 'Adī:

"Reclining, whose doors are knocked upon, a servant serves over him with the kūb."

Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Zukhruf.

﴿Crystal-clear glass, crystal of silver﴾: i.e. in the description of the glass, in clarity and in the whiteness of silver. Its clarity is the clarity of glass, and its color is the color of silver.

Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī, and Abū Bakr read (qawārīra qawārīra) with tanwīn on both with pause and connection, and with pausing on both with an alif. The aspect of this reading has already been given in the explanation of His saying (salāsil, "chains") in this surah, and we explained there the reason for declining what has the form of the final plural pattern, so return to it.

Ḥamzah read without tanwīn on both and without pausing with an alif. The aspect of this reading is clear, since both are excluded from declension by the form of the final plural pattern.

Hishām read without tanwīn on both with pausing on both with an alif. Ibn Kathīr read with tanwīn on the first without the second, and pausing on the first with an alif without the second.

Abū 'Amr, Ḥafṣ, and Ibn Dhakwān read without tanwīn on both, and pausing on the first with an alif, not the second. The clause is in the genitive position as an attribute of (akwāb, "goblets").

Abū al-Baqā' said: The repetition is good because of what is attached to it, namely the explanation of its origin.

al-Wāḥidī said: The exegetes said: God made the glass of the people of Paradise of silver, so there combined for it the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Zajjāj said: The glass that is in this world is made of sand, and God informed us of the excellence of that glass, that its origin is silver, so that what is inside it is seen from its outside.

The clause ﴿they have measured it with measure﴾ is an attribute of (qawārīr, "glass").

The majority read (qaddarūhā, "they measured it") with a fatḥah on the qāf, in the active voice: i.e. the servers, from among the attendants who go around them, measured it according to what the drinkers of the people of Paradise need, without excess or deficiency.

Mujāhid and others said: they brought it according to their measure of satisfaction, without excess or deficiency.

Al-Kalbī said: That is more delicious and more appetizing. It was also said: the angels measured it. It was also said: the people of Paradise, the drinkers, measured it according to the measure of their desires and needs, so it came as they wanted in form, neither exceeding nor falling short.

ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sulamī, al-Sha'bī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Abū ʿAmr in one narration from him read (quddirūhā) with a ḍammah on the qāf and a kasrah on the dāl, in the passive voice: i.e. it was made for them according to their desire.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: This is of the type of inversion (qalb). He said: because the real meaning is that it should be said: "it was measured for them", not "they measured it", since it has the meaning of "they were measured for it."

Abū Ḥātim said: The measure: the vessels were measured according to the measure of their satisfaction, so the object of the passive, its subject, is omitted.

Abū Ḥayyān said: The closer explanation for the derivation of this irregular reading is to say: "their satisfaction was measured from it, a measure", so the genitive noun is omitted and it became (quddirū hā).

Al-Mahdawī said: the meaning of the last reading returns to the meaning of the first reading, and it seems that the original was (qadarū 'alayhā), then the prepositional particle was omitted, as Sībawayh recited:

"I swore I would not eat the love of Iraq as long as the years last, and love in the village is eaten by the weevil."

That is: "I swore upon the love of Iraq."

﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: it has already been stated that the cup is the vessel that contains wine, and if it is empty of wine it is not called a cup. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will be given to drink in Paradise a cup of wine mixed with ginger, and the Arabs used to enjoy mixing drink with ginger for the pleasantness of its fragrance.

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: Zanjabīl is the name of a spring from which those brought near (al-muqarrabūn) drink.

Muqātil said: It is ginger, but not like the ginger of this world.

﴿A spring therein named Salsabīl﴾: the accusative of (ʿaynan, "a spring") is that it is an apposition (badal) from (kaʾsan, "a cup"). It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by an omitted verb: i.e. "they are given to drink a spring." It is permissible that it be in the accusative by removal of the preposition: i.e. "from a spring." Al-salsabīl is the delicious drink, derived from al-salāsah (smoothness). The Arabs say: "this is a smooth drink (sharāb salis)", and "salsāl" and "salsabīl", i.e. good and delicious.

Al-Zajjāj said: Salsabīl in the language is the name of water in extreme smoothness, sharp in its flow, which goes down easily in their throats. From this is the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

"They are given to drink from the flow of al-Barīṣ over them, a cup that clinks with the smooth, sealed wine (al-raḥīq al-salsal)."

﴿And there will go around them youths made eternal﴾: when He, glory be to Him, finished describing their drink, and the description of their vessels, and the description of the servers who give them that drink.

The meaning of (mukhalladūn, "made eternal") is that they remain as they are in youth, freshness, and radiance, not aging nor changing. It was also said: the meaning of mukhalladūn is that they do not die. It was also said: takhlīd means adornment, i.e. they are adorned.

﴿When you see them, you think them scattered pearls﴾: when you look at them, you suppose them, because of their great beauty, the clarity of their colors, and the brightness of their faces, scattered pearls, unstrung.

ʿAṭāʾ said: He means in whiteness of color and its beauty, and pearls when scattered from the string on a carpet are finer than when strung.

The people of meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: They were only compared to scattered pearls because they scatter about in service, and if they were in rows they would have been compared to strung pearls. It was also said: He compared them to scattered pearls because they are swift in service, unlike the dark-eyed houris, for He compared them to hidden pearls, because they are not degraded by service.

﴿And when you look there, you see bliss and a great dominion﴾: i.e. and when you cast your sight there, meaning in the Garden, you see bliss that cannot be described, and a great dominion whose measure cannot be estimated. (Thamma, "there") is a noun of place, and its governing element is (ra'ayta, "you see").

Al-Farrā' said: in the speech there is an implied (mā), i.e. "and when you see what is there", like His saying: ﴿Surely your connection has been cut﴾ [al-An'ām: 94], i.e. what is between you.

Al-Zajjāj objected to al-Farrā', saying: it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave out the relative clause, but (ra'ayta) transitively reaches (thamma) in meaning. The meaning is: "when you see with your sight there", and by (thamma) he means the Garden.

Al-Suddī said: bliss is what one enjoys, and the great dominion is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. Muqātil and al-Kalbī said the same.

It was also said that (ra'ayta) has no object, neither spoken, nor implied, nor intended; rather its meaning is: wherever your sight falls in the Garden, you see bliss and a great dominion.

﴿Above them are garments of green silk﴾: Nāfi', Ḥamzah, and Ibn Muḥaysin read (ʿāliyahum) with a sukūn on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ, as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and (thiyāb, "garments") as a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), or (ʿāliyahum) is a subject (mubtada'), and (thiyāb) is in the nominative as the agent of the attribute, even though the attribute does not depend on a preceding element, as is the view of al-Akhfash.

Al-Farrā' said: It is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (thiyāb sundus), and the active participle is meant as a plural.

The rest read with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the hāʾ, as an adverbial of place (ẓarf) in the nominative position as a predicate placed first, and (thiyāb) as a postponed subject, as if it had been said: "above them are garments."

Al-Farrā' said: (ʿāliyahum) means "above them", and so said Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.

Abū Ḥayyān said: ʿālin and ʿāliyah are active participles, so for them to be adverbs of place they would need to be transmitted from the speech of the Arabs. Rather it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of two things: the first is the hāʾ and mīm in His saying ﴿circulate among them﴾, i.e. around the righteous, (wildān, "youths") are high above the righteous, (thiyāb sundus, "garments of green silk"), i.e. they go around them in this state.

The second is that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the youths: i.e. when you see them you suppose them scattered pearls while the garments are above their bodies.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the governing element of the circumstantial qualifier is either (laqqāhum naḍratan wa-surūran, "He gave them radiance and joy") or (jazāhum bi-mā ṣabarū, "He rewarded them for what they endured"). He said: it is also permissible that it be an adverb of place.

Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, because of the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: ʿāliyatuhum.

The majority read (thiyāb, "garments") with an annexation to (sundus).

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read (thiyābun) with tanwīn and cutting it off from the annexation, and (sundusun) in the nominative. And (khuḍrun wa-istabraq, "green and brocade") are: the sundus is an attribute of the garments, because sundus is a kind of garment; and (khuḍr) is an attribute of sundus, because it may be green and not green; and (istabraq) is coordinated with sundus, i.e. "and garments of brocade."

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read (khuḍarun) in the nominative as an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqin) in the genitive as an attribute of sundus.

Abū Ḥātim and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this reading, because (khuḍr) is best when it is an attribute of garments, so it is in the nominative, and brocade is of the same kind as sundus.

Nāfi' and Ḥafṣ read ﴿green and brocade﴾ in the nominative, because (khuḍrun) is an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqun) is coordinated with (thiyāb).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: az-zamharir is the severe cold.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Fire complained to its Lord, saying: 'My Lord, some of me has consumed others of me.' So He allowed it two breaths: a breath in summer and a breath in winter. Therefore, the intense cold you feel is from its zamharir, and the intense heat you feel in summer is from its samum."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad ibn al-Sari, Abd ibn Humayd, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib regarding His words ﴿And near them will be its shade﴾ that he said: close. ﴿And its fruit will be lowered in readiness﴾ he said: The people of the Garden eat from the fruits of the Garden standing, sitting, and reclining, and in whatever state they wish.

In another wording he said: it is made submissive, so they take from it however they wish.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "vessels of silver whose clearness is like the clearness of glass" ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾: he said: they were measured for the hand.

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until you made it like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen through it; but the glass of Paradise is the whiteness of silver with the clearness of glass.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also: There is nothing in Paradise except that you have been given its likeness in this world, except glass made of silver.

Al-Firyabi narrated from him also regarding His words ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾ he said: They are brought in a measure suited to the mouth; they do not prefer anything, nor desire anything after it.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him also: ﴿they will determine its measure well﴾ he said: the cup-bearers determined it.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Amr who said: The lowest in rank among the people of Paradise is one whom a thousand servants attend, each servant occupied with a task which its master does not have. He recited this verse: ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾.

His saying: ﴿reclining therein upon couches﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the object of (jazāhum, "rewarded them"). The governing element is (jazā, "rewarded"), and "patient" (ṣabarū) does not govern it, because patience was only in this world. Abū al-Baqā' permitted that it be an attribute of (jannah, "garden").

Al-Farrā' said: If you wish, you may make (muttaki'īn, "reclining") a follower (tābi'), as if he had said: "He rewarded them with a garden, reclining therein."

Al-Akhfash said: It may be in the accusative by way of praise (madḥ), and the pronoun in (fīhā, "therein") refers to the garden. Al-arā'ik (the couches) are the thrones within canopies (ḥijāl), and their explanation has already been given in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿They see therein no sun nor freezing cold (zamharīr)﴾: the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the object of (jazāhum), so it is among the successive circumstantial qualifiers (al-ḥāl al-mutarādifah), or it is from the pronoun in (muttaki'īn), so it is among the interlocking circumstantial qualifiers (al-ḥāl al-mutadākhilah), or it is another attribute of the garden. Al-zamharīr is the most intense cold. The meaning is that they do not see in the Garden the heat of the sun nor the cold of zamharīr. From this is the saying of al-A'shā:

"Pampered, a young girl, like a gazelle; she has not seen sun nor zamharīr."

Tha'lab said: Al-zamharīr is the moon in the dialect of Ṭayyi', and he recited a verse of their poet:

"And a night whose darkness has gathered thick, I crossed it while the zamharīr had not shone."

It is also narrated as "had not appeared", meaning the moon had not risen. The explanation of this has already been given in Surat Maryam.

﴿And near over them are its shades﴾: the majority of readers read (dāniyatan, "near") in the accusative, as a coordination with the position of (lā yarawna, "they do not see"), or with (muttaki'īn), or as an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e. "and a garden near", as if he had said: "and He rewarded them with a near garden."

Al-Zajjāj said: It is an attribute of the previously mentioned "garden."

Al-Farrā' said: It is in the accusative by way of praise.

Abū Ḥaywah read (wa-dāniyatun, "and near") in the nominative, as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), with (ẓilāluhā, "its shades") as a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier.

The meaning: the shadows of the trees are close to them, shading over them, as an increase in their bliss, even though there is no sun there.

Muqātil said: It means its trees are near them.

Ibn Mas'ūd read (wa-dāniyan 'alayhim), "and near over them."

﴿Its fruit-clusters are made easy to reach, with complete ease﴾: it is coordinated with (dāniyatan), as if he had said: "and made easy (muzallalah)." It is permissible that the clause be in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ('alayhim), and it is permissible that it be a new independent sentence. Al-quṭūf are the fruits. The meaning is that its fruits have been made subservient to those who pick them, with very great subservience, such that one who stands, sits, or lies down can take them, and neither distance nor thorn turns their hands away from them.

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-mudhallal is that which is near to hand and easy to reach. From this is their saying: "a low wall" (ḥā'iṭun dhalīl), i.e. short.

Ibn Qutaybah said: dhullilat means "brought near", from their saying "a low wall", i.e. it was short in height. It was also said: dhullilat means made submissive, not resisting those who pick them however they wish.

﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and goblets﴾: i.e. servants go around them when they want drink, with vessels of silver. Al-akwāb is the plural of kūb, which is a large jug with no handle nor loop. From this is the saying of 'Adī:

"Reclining, whose doors are knocked upon, a servant serves over him with the kūb."

Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Zukhruf.

﴿Crystal-clear glass, crystal of silver﴾: i.e. in the description of the glass, in clarity and in the whiteness of silver. Its clarity is the clarity of glass, and its color is the color of silver.

Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī, and Abū Bakr read (qawārīra qawārīra) with tanwīn on both with pause and connection, and with pausing on both with an alif. The aspect of this reading has already been given in the explanation of His saying (salāsil, "chains") in this surah, and we explained there the reason for declining what has the form of the final plural pattern, so return to it.

Ḥamzah read without tanwīn on both and without pausing with an alif. The aspect of this reading is clear, since both are excluded from declension by the form of the final plural pattern.

Hishām read without tanwīn on both with pausing on both with an alif. Ibn Kathīr read with tanwīn on the first without the second, and pausing on the first with an alif without the second.

Abū 'Amr, Ḥafṣ, and Ibn Dhakwān read without tanwīn on both, and pausing on the first with an alif, not the second. The clause is in the genitive position as an attribute of (akwāb, "goblets").

Abū al-Baqā' said: The repetition is good because of what is attached to it, namely the explanation of its origin.

al-Wāḥidī said: The exegetes said: God made the glass of the people of Paradise of silver, so there combined for it the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

Al-Zajjāj said: The glass that is in this world is made of sand, and God informed us of the excellence of that glass, that its origin is silver, so that what is inside it is seen from its outside.

The clause ﴿they have measured it with measure﴾ is an attribute of (qawārīr, "glass").

The majority read (qaddarūhā, "they measured it") with a fatḥah on the qāf, in the active voice: i.e. the servers, from among the attendants who go around them, measured it according to what the drinkers of the people of Paradise need, without excess or deficiency.

Mujāhid and others said: they brought it according to their measure of satisfaction, without excess or deficiency.

Al-Kalbī said: That is more delicious and more appetizing. It was also said: the angels measured it. It was also said: the people of Paradise, the drinkers, measured it according to the measure of their desires and needs, so it came as they wanted in form, neither exceeding nor falling short.

ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sulamī, al-Sha'bī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Abū ʿAmr in one narration from him read (quddirūhā) with a ḍammah on the qāf and a kasrah on the dāl, in the passive voice: i.e. it was made for them according to their desire.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: This is of the type of inversion (qalb). He said: because the real meaning is that it should be said: "it was measured for them", not "they measured it", since it has the meaning of "they were measured for it."

Abū Ḥātim said: The measure: the vessels were measured according to the measure of their satisfaction, so the object of the passive, its subject, is omitted.

Abū Ḥayyān said: The closer explanation for the derivation of this irregular reading is to say: "their satisfaction was measured from it, a measure", so the genitive noun is omitted and it became (quddirū hā).

Al-Mahdawī said: the meaning of the last reading returns to the meaning of the first reading, and it seems that the original was (qadarū 'alayhā), then the prepositional particle was omitted, as Sībawayh recited:

"I swore I would not eat the love of Iraq as long as the years last, and love in the village is eaten by the weevil."

That is: "I swore upon the love of Iraq."

﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾: it has already been stated that the cup is the vessel that contains wine, and if it is empty of wine it is not called a cup. The meaning is that the people of Paradise will be given to drink in Paradise a cup of wine mixed with ginger, and the Arabs used to enjoy mixing drink with ginger for the pleasantness of its fragrance.

Mujāhid and Qatādah said: Zanjabīl is the name of a spring from which those brought near (al-muqarrabūn) drink.

Muqātil said: It is ginger, but not like the ginger of this world.

﴿A spring therein named Salsabīl﴾: the accusative of (ʿaynan, "a spring") is that it is an apposition (badal) from (kaʾsan, "a cup"). It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by an omitted verb: i.e. "they are given to drink a spring." It is permissible that it be in the accusative by removal of the preposition: i.e. "from a spring." Al-salsabīl is the delicious drink, derived from al-salāsah (smoothness). The Arabs say: "this is a smooth drink (sharāb salis)", and "salsāl" and "salsabīl", i.e. good and delicious.

Al-Zajjāj said: Salsabīl in the language is the name of water in extreme smoothness, sharp in its flow, which goes down easily in their throats. From this is the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

"They are given to drink from the flow of al-Barīṣ over them, a cup that clinks with the smooth, sealed wine (al-raḥīq al-salsal)."

﴿And there will go around them youths made eternal﴾: when He, glory be to Him, finished describing their drink, and the description of their vessels, and the description of the servers who give them that drink.

The meaning of (mukhalladūn, "made eternal") is that they remain as they are in youth, freshness, and radiance, not aging nor changing. It was also said: the meaning of mukhalladūn is that they do not die. It was also said: takhlīd means adornment, i.e. they are adorned.

﴿When you see them, you think them scattered pearls﴾: when you look at them, you suppose them, because of their great beauty, the clarity of their colors, and the brightness of their faces, scattered pearls, unstrung.

ʿAṭāʾ said: He means in whiteness of color and its beauty, and pearls when scattered from the string on a carpet are finer than when strung.

The people of meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: They were only compared to scattered pearls because they scatter about in service, and if they were in rows they would have been compared to strung pearls. It was also said: He compared them to scattered pearls because they are swift in service, unlike the dark-eyed houris, for He compared them to hidden pearls, because they are not degraded by service.

﴿And when you look there, you see bliss and a great dominion﴾: i.e. and when you cast your sight there, meaning in the Garden, you see bliss that cannot be described, and a great dominion whose measure cannot be estimated. (Thamma, "there") is a noun of place, and its governing element is (ra'ayta, "you see").

Al-Farrā' said: in the speech there is an implied (mā), i.e. "and when you see what is there", like His saying: ﴿Surely your connection has been cut﴾ [al-An'ām: 94], i.e. what is between you.

Al-Zajjāj objected to al-Farrā', saying: it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave out the relative clause, but (ra'ayta) transitively reaches (thamma) in meaning. The meaning is: "when you see with your sight there", and by (thamma) he means the Garden.

Al-Suddī said: bliss is what one enjoys, and the great dominion is the angels' seeking permission to enter upon them. Muqātil and al-Kalbī said the same.

It was also said that (ra'ayta) has no object, neither spoken, nor implied, nor intended; rather its meaning is: wherever your sight falls in the Garden, you see bliss and a great dominion.

﴿Above them are garments of green silk﴾: Nāfi', Ḥamzah, and Ibn Muḥaysin read (ʿāliyahum) with a sukūn on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the hāʾ, as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and (thiyāb, "garments") as a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), or (ʿāliyahum) is a subject (mubtada'), and (thiyāb) is in the nominative as the agent of the attribute, even though the attribute does not depend on a preceding element, as is the view of al-Akhfash.

Al-Farrā' said: It is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (thiyāb sundus), and the active participle is meant as a plural.

The rest read with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and a ḍammah on the hāʾ, as an adverbial of place (ẓarf) in the nominative position as a predicate placed first, and (thiyāb) as a postponed subject, as if it had been said: "above them are garments."

Al-Farrā' said: (ʿāliyahum) means "above them", and so said Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.

Abū Ḥayyān said: ʿālin and ʿāliyah are active participles, so for them to be adverbs of place they would need to be transmitted from the speech of the Arabs. Al-Zajjāj had already preceded him in this and said: "This is something we do not know in adverbs. Had it been an adverb, why would it not be permissible to make the yāʾ quiescent?" Rather it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of two things: the first is the hāʾ and mīm in His saying ﴿circulate among them﴾, i.e. around the righteous, (wildān, "youths") are high above the righteous, (thiyāb sundus, "garments of green silk"), i.e. they go around them in this state.

The second is that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the youths: i.e. when you see them you suppose them scattered pearls while the garments are above their bodies.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the governing element of the circumstantial qualifier is either (laqqāhum naḍratan wa-surūran, "He gave them radiance and joy") or (jazāhum bi-mā ṣabarū, "He rewarded them for what they endured"). He said: it is also permissible that it be an adverb of place.

Ibn Sīrīn, Mujāhid, Abū Ḥaywah, and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read ʿalayhim, "over them", a reading clear in meaning and evident in indication.

Abū ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, because of the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: ʿāliyatuhum.

The majority read (thiyāb, "garments") with an annexation to (sundus).

Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read (thiyābun) with tanwīn and cutting it off from the annexation, and (sundusun) in the nominative. And (khuḍrun wa-istabraq, "green and brocade") are: the sundus is an attribute of the garments, because sundus is a kind of garment; and (khuḍr) is an attribute of sundus, because it may be green and not green; and (istabraq) is coordinated with sundus, i.e. "and garments of brocade."

The majority of readers differed over ﴿green and brocade﴾, while agreeing on the genitive of sundus through the annexation of (thiyāb) to it. Ibn Kathīr, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Muḥaysin read (khuḍrin) in the genitive as an attribute of (sundus), and (istabraqu) in the nominative, coordinated with (thiyāb): i.e. "upon them are garments of sundus, and upon them is brocade."

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read (khuḍarun) in the nominative as an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqin) in the genitive as an attribute of sundus.

Abū Ḥātim and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this reading, because (khuḍr) is best when it is an attribute of garments, so it is in the nominative, and brocade is of the same kind as sundus.

Nāfi' and Ḥafṣ read ﴿green and brocade﴾ in the nominative, because (khuḍrun) is an attribute of (thiyāb), and (istabraqun) is coordinated with (thiyāb).

Al-Farra' and Abu Qilaba... Let me produce the translation.

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "khudrin wa-istabraqin" with the genitive (jarr), taking "khudrin" as an adjective (na't) of "sundus" and "istabraqin" as conjoined (ma'tuf) to "sundus."

All of them read "istabraqin" with tanwin (ṣarf), except Ibn Muhaysin, who did not give it tanwin. He said: "Because it is a foreign (a'jami) word." There is no basis for this, because it is indefinite (nakira), unless he means that it is a proper name ( 'alam) for this kind of garment.

Al-sundus (fine silk brocade) is what is thin of ad-dibaj (silk brocade). Al-istabraq is what is thick of it. Their meanings were already explained in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yatufu 'alayhim" (they will be served by youths circulating among them).

Here, He, glorified is He, mentions that they will be adorned with bracelets of silver. In Surat Fatir, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [Fatir: 33], and in Surat al-Hajj, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾ [al-Hajj: 23]. There is no contradiction between these verses, since they can be reconciled: either He gives them bracelets of gold, silver and pearls together, or the meaning is that they wear bracelets of gold at one time, bracelets of silver at another, and bracelets of pearls at another, or each person wears of them what his soul inclines to. It is also permissible for this sentence to be in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "'aliyahum," with "qad" implied.

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: this is another kind of drink with which Allah bestows favor upon them.

Al-Farra' said: It means it is pure, not impure, as it was in the world, where it was described as impure.

The meaning is that this drink is pure, unlike the wine of this world.

Muqatil said: It is a spring at the gate of the Garden; whoever drinks from it, Allah removes from his heart whatever deceit, rancor and envy it contained.

Abu Qilaba and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: They are brought food, and when it is finished they bring the pure drink, so they drink, and their stomachs become lean from it, and sweat flows from their bodies like the scent of musk.

﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward﴾: that is, it is said to them: this which has been mentioned of kinds of blessings has been for you a reward for your deeds, that is, a recompense for them. ﴿And your effort has been appreciated﴾: that is, your deeds in the world in obedience to Allah were accepted and approved. Allah's appreciation of His servant's deed is His acceptance of his obedience.

So He allowed it two breaths: a breath in summer and a breath in winter. Therefore, the intense cold you feel is from its zamharir, and the intense heat you feel in summer is from its samum."
